text: James F. Mulhern - Instructor Biography Silver Current Press INSTRUCTOR BIOGRAPHY · ONE PAGE James F. Mulhern Novelist · Professor Emeritus of English · Oxford Writing Fellow · Founder, Silver Current Press James F. Mulhern is a Kirkus-starred novelist, short story writer, and poet. His novel Give Them Unquiet Dreams received a starred review from Kirkus Reviews and was named one of Kirkus's Best Books of 2019. His fiction has been nominated for a Pushcart Prize, and his poetry has been shortlisted for the Aesthetica Creative Writing Award. In 2015 Exeter College at the University of Oxford awarded him a fully funded Writing Fellowship, an unusually competitive honor for a mid-career American writer. He is the author of eight books — Give Them Unquiet Dreams, Molly Bonamici, The Weight of Small Mercies, All We Ever Needed, Mia Bambina and Other Stories, Crossings, and companion volumes in publishing and craft — available on Amazon and through Silver Current Press. Mr. Mulhern taught English for more than thirty years — in secondary and college classrooms, as a department chair, and as a mentor to writers at every level. Now Professor Emeritus, he directs his practice toward the most useful next chapter for a writer with his years and credentials: teaching adults to read and write serious literature, together, in the format that first made him love the work — the salon. He is the founder of Silver Current Press, a Philadelphia literary imprint, and the author of a working catalog of twelve courses — American, Irish, Jewish, and minority literary traditions; women writers; poetry and Shakespeare; memoir; and the craft of writing itself. Every course can be delivered as a sixteen-session series, a shorter four-session workshop, or a single evening talk, in person or on Zoom. text: Frequently Asked Questions for Program Partners The 2601 Salon · Silver Current Press FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS · FOR PROGRAM PARTNERS Bringing a Salon Course to Your Community Everything a program director needs to know, in one document. What the courses are. Who they're for. How to book. What it costs. What you supply. What I supply. And every reasonable question in between. James F. Mulhern Kirkus-starred novelist · Oxford Writing Fellow · Professor Emeritus of English salon.silvercurrentpress.com/partners.html IF YOU'D RATHER JUST TALK Email jamesfmulhern@gmail.com. Fifteen minutes on the phone will tell us both whether there is a fit. First offering at a new venue is at no cost as a proof of concept. Page 1 of 5 Frequently Asked Questions for Program Partners The 2601 Salon · Silver Current Press QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS THE COURSES What courses can I book? Twelve. The full catalog is at salon.silvercurrentpress.com/partners.html. They include five literary surveys (American Literature; Women in American Literature; Minority Voices; Jewish Writers; Irish Literature), one interdisciplinary course (Literature and American History), two reading workshops (Poetry; Shakespeare's Sonnets and Speeches), three writing workshops (Memoir; Revision; The Writing Life), and one master salon (The Art of Telling). Every course can also be built to spec for a specific occasion — a Joyce weekend for a museum, a Chekhov masterclass for a writers' conference, and so on. How long is a course? Any of them can be a full sixteen-session series, a shorter four-to-eight-session workshop, or a single 60–90 minute evening lecture. The Art of Telling is a ten-session salon. Length is shaped to your calendar and audience, not to my convenience. Where can it be delivered? In person or on Zoom. Hybrid works too. In-person locations include libraries, bookstores, community centers, universities, retirement communities, museums, and literary nonprofits, primarily in the Philadelphia region. Zoom courses work anywhere in the world. What does a typical session look like? Ninety minutes, discussion-based, no lecture podium. We read a short published text together, ask three or four honest questions of it, and let the room work. There are no quizzes, papers, or grades. Every session is generous, close, and non-competitive. YOUR AUDIENCE Who are these courses for? Adult readers and writers who are not looking for a degree. The audience I've been teaching for years is thoughtful adults who read seriously and want more than a book club can give them. Retirees, mid-career professionals, empty-nesters, lifelong learners, people who miss a college English seminar and want it back. The reading load is modest and the discussion is generous. Do participants need to have read a lot of literature? No. All of my courses are designed so that a curious adult who has never taken an English course beyond high school can walk in and be at home in the room within the first ten minutes. The reading workshops (Poetry, Shakespeare) are especially designed for people who have always suspected they were supposed to like these things but somehow never did. Page 2 of 5 Frequently Asked Questions for Program Partners The 2601 Salon · Silver Current Press What's the ideal group size? Twelve to twenty-five participants in person; up to forty on Zoom. Smaller groups (six to twelve) produce the deepest conversations. Larger groups (twenty-five to forty) work well when the format is more lecture-plus-discussion. I can adapt to whatever your venue and audience produce. COST AND LOGISTICS What does it cost? For a first offering at a new venue, I'm glad to teach at no cost as a proof of concept for both of us. Ongoing terms are set to fit the host. That can be an honorarium, a per-session fee, a revenue share on a paid course, or grant-funded — whatever fits your operating model. I'm easy to work with. What does the host supply? A room and its promotion, or the equivalent Zoom platform. That's it. All course materials, syllabi, reading lists, and discussion frameworks are on my side. I bring my own laptop and, when needed, my own projector. How does enrollment work? Handled entirely by your organization. I don't collect fees, addresses, or personal information from participants. Your venue's normal registration process is the one we use. What about accessibility? The courses are non-graded, non-competitive, and non-technical. Every reading is either public domain or freely accessible online through Project Gutenberg, the Internet Archive, the Poetry Foundation, and similar sources. Zoom sessions can be captioned via the built-in tool. For in-person sessions, I follow the venue's accessibility standards. MATERIALS AND COPYRIGHT What reading materials are used? Every reading is either public domain or freely available online. No participant needs to buy a book. Where a longer work is helpful, it's linked to the Internet Archive's controlled digital lending program (a free account borrows any book for an hour at a time). For copyrighted poems and short stories, links go to the Poetry Foundation, Poets.org, and other legitimate free hosts. Can we reuse your syllabi or reading lists? Yes, with a short note. Institutional and classroom use is welcome; a one-line email to jamesfmulhern@gmail.com is enough. For most partners the answer is a warm yes with an attribution line. I ask only because material like this can otherwise disappear into commercial course kits with no attribution. Can we record the sessions? Yes, if the participants and I both agree in advance. Zoom sessions can be recorded and made available to your audience for a limited window. In-person recording is possible with venue and participant permission. ABOUT THE INSTRUCTOR Page 3 of 5 Frequently Asked Questions for Program Partners The 2601 Salon · Silver Current Press Who is teaching? James F. Mulhern. Kirkus-starred novelist (Give Them Unquiet Dreams was starred by Kirkus and named a Kirkus Best Book of 2019). Oxford Writing Fellow (fully funded fellowship at Exeter College, University of Oxford). Pushcart Prize nomination in fiction. Aesthetica Creative Writing Award shortlist in poetry. Professor Emeritus of English with more than thirty years of college and secondary teaching. Founder of Silver Current Press, an independent literary imprint in Philadelphia. How can I verify these credentials? The Kirkus starred review is at kirkusreviews.com. The Amazon Author Page lists all eight books. The author site (authorjamesmulhern.com) has the press kit, a full biography, and interviews. All of these are linked from the partners page. Feel free to reach out to any of them independently. What's your teaching style? Discussion-based, generous, unhurried. I do not lecture down to a room. I open the material and let the room work with it. I assume intelligence. I take questions seriously. Nothing said in the room is repeated outside it. The best sessions I have ever taught happened wherever a serious group of adults sat down together with a shared text. NEXT STEPS How do I book a course? Send me an email at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com. Tell me which course you're interested in, roughly when you'd like to offer it, and what your venue can accommodate. I usually reply within a day. Fifteen minutes on the phone tells both of us whether there is a fit. What if the fit isn't right? That's entirely fine. Program directors often know a colleague or a peer organization who would be a better match, and a warm introduction from you is one of the most useful things I can receive. If the fit isn't right this year but might be next year, we can put it on a soft calendar and revisit. Page 4 of 5 Frequently Asked Questions for Program Partners The 2601 Salon · Silver Current Press Ready to talk? Fifteen minutes will tell us both whether there is a fit. Email: jamesfmulhern@gmail.com The partners page: salon.silvercurrentpress.com/partners.html Course catalog: salon.silvercurrentpress.com The author's site: authorjamesmulhern.com Kirkus starred review: kirkusreviews.com/book-reviews/james-mulhern/give-them-unquiet-dreams/ IF NOT NOW, MAYBE LATER If the fit isn't right this season, I'd welcome a note anyway. Program directors who like the work but can't host this quarter are one of my best resources — a warm introduction to a colleague at another venue is worth more than a booking. And if I'm just early for your calendar, put this on a soft calendar and I'll write again in six months. Page 5 of 5

literary salon for adult readers and writers, taught by James F. Mulhern — Professor of English and recipient of a Writing Fellowship at Exeter College, University of Oxford. Professor Mulhern is also a published novelist, short story writer, poet, and essayist. The Courses Click any course to see its full syllabus, readings, and sessions. Survey of American Literature Sixteen Sessions › A chronological journey from Indigenous voices and Puritan sermons to contemporary American writing — read slowly, together. Women in American Literature Sixteen Sessions › From Anne Bradstreet and Phillis Wheatley to Toni Morrison and Joy Harjo — a chronological reading of the women whose work makes the American canon whole. Minority Voices in American Literature Sixteen Sessions › Black, Latinx, Asian American, Native American, and immigrant voices — from Frederick Douglass to Ocean Vuong — read with the close attention they have always deserved. Jewish Writers: A Literary Tradition Sixteen Sessions › Sholem Aleichem, Kafka, Singer, Primo Levi, Celan, Bellow, Malamud, Ozick, Paley, Amichai — a literature older than empires, read together. The Irish Literary Imagination Sixteen Sessions › Sixteen weeks of Irish writing — from the Táin and Swift to Yeats, Joyce, Heaney, Boland, and the contemporary moment. Personal territory for your instructor. Literature & American History — A Cross-Reading Sixteen Sessions › Each week pairs a primary historical document with the literary work answering it — the Declaration with Douglass, the 14th Amendment with Du Bois, the Pentagon Papers with O'Brien. Reading Poetry: A Beginner's Welcome Sixteen Sessions › An unhurried introduction to poetry for anyone who has ever felt locked out of it. We read aloud, we sit with the lines, and we discover that a poem is not a code to crack. Shakespeare's Sonnets & Famous Speeches Sixteen Sessions › Sixteen sonnets paired with sixteen of Shakespeare's most famous monologues — short, self-contained texts read aloud and discussed. No full plays, no homework dread. The Personal Essay & Memoir Sixteen Sessions › Writing from a life — your own. We read masters of the form and we write by hand, in scene, with candor and craft. The Craft of Revision — A Writers' Workshop Sixteen Sessions › Bring your pages. We will read them aloud, cut them, sharpen them, and send them out. The Writing Life: Getting Published Sixteen Sessions › The literary magazine scene, cover letters and queries, agents, small presses, contests — the practical work of becoming a published writer, taught by a working writer and former editor. The Art of Telling Ten Sessions › A salon in short story, poetry, and memoir. Ten Sundays across the three great narrative forms — the course that gave the salon its name, now on the shelf beside the others. How Chekhov Ends Four Sessions › A close-reading workshop on the last paragraph of the modern short story. Four Chekhov stories, read slowly, with attention to the ending Chekhov taught fiction how to make. Joyce's Sentences Two Sessions › A close-reading weekend on the last pages of The Dead and on Molly Bloom's soliloquy at the end of Ulysses. Two of the most famous passages in modern English prose, read aloud and slowly. Reading Emerson Four Sessions › Four Emerson essays read slowly — Nature, Self-Reliance, The American Scholar, and Circles. The founding voice of American thought, at the pace he asks to be read. Reading Dickinson Four Sessions › Emily Dickinson at close range — the dashes, the slant rhymes, the small rooms that hold whole universes. Twenty-four of her finest poems, unhurried. Reading Thoreau Four Sessions › Walden and Civil Disobedience, read as literature and as challenge. Three sessions in the cabin at the pond, one in the Concord jail. Reading Whitman Four Sessions › Song of Myself in three unhurried passes, then the Civil War poems that gave Whitman his deepest music. Read aloud, always. The Presidential Speech Six Sessions › Six great American speeches close-read for their craft, rhetorical devices, and historical context. Washington's Farewell, Lincoln's Second Inaugural, FDR, JFK, Dr. King, and Reagan on the Challenger. Our Building, Our Story: Writing the Life of 2601 Ten Sessions · For 2601 Residents › A course written for our own building — craft fundamentals, the ethics of writing about real neighbors, and the arrival, portrait, happy, hard, and funniest-experience essays that become a shared, publishable resident anthology. About This Salon The 2601 Salon is a literary program of Silver Current Press — a working catalog of the courses Professor Mulhern is prepared to teach for adult readers and writers. Every course meets weekly for ninety minutes. There are no grades, no quizzes, and no prerequisites — only an invitation to sit with serious books, to talk about them in plain language, and to improve one's own writing along the way. These courses are about both literature and the craft of writing. Each course is shaped the same way: a brief historical framing at the top of the hour, a passage read aloud, a guided discussion around four to six open questions, and an optional ten-minute writing prompt at the close. Any device with a browser suffices for in-class access to the readings. Writing in class, however, is always done by hand. We have found this matters. Readings are open-access. Most are in the public domain and are linked from each course page; the remainder are available as free digital borrows through the Internet Archive. About the Instructor James F. Mulhern is a Philadelphia novelist and Professor Emeritus of English. His novel Give Them Unquiet Dreams received a Kirkus starred review and was named a Kirkus Best Book of 2019. He held a fully funded Writing Fellowship at Exeter College, University of Oxford; was nominated for a Pushcart Prize; and was shortlisted for the Aesthetica Creative Writing Award. He served as Department Chair in both English and Social Studies and as an AP Consultant for the College Board and the National Math and Science Initiative. He is the founder of Silver Current Press, a Philadelphia literary imprint. Full biography at authorjamesmulhern.com . Formats & Availability Courses are offered in three formats, and Professor Mulhern will adapt any of the courses in this catalog to fit a partner venue's calendar and audience. In person — at libraries, bookstores, community centers, universities, retirement communities, and literary nonprofits in the Philadelphia region and, on request, elsewhere in the Northeast. Online — by Zoom or comparable platform, to any group of adult readers anywhere. Hybrid — a combination of in-person sessions and online continuation, tailored to the host. Full sixteen-session courses, four-session workshops, single evening talks, and one-day masterclasses are all available. Please write with your calendar and I will propose a shape that fits. How to Enroll or Book a Course Individual learners — if you would like to attend a course, express interest in a future session, or receive occasional announcements about new offerings, please write to me at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . There is no formal enrollment. Program directors, librarians, and venue partners — if you host adult programming and would like to bring a course to your community, please write to jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . Please include the venue, an approximate audience size, and a proposed date window; terms are set to fit the host. Mulhern for Silver Current Press. Readers are always welcome to read, print, share, and quote these pages for their own study and enjoyment. That is what the site is for. Mulhern Novelist · Professor Emeritus of English · Oxford Writing Fellow · Founder of Silver Current Press James F. Mulhern has spent his working life inside two disciplines that reinforce each other: the disciplined reading of literature, and the disciplined making of it. He taught English for more than three decades — in secondary and college classrooms, as a department chair, and as a mentor to writers at every level from apprentice to publishing professional. His novels and short fiction have received a Kirkus Starred Review, a place on Kirkus’s Best Books of 2019 list, a Pushcart Prize nomination in fiction, and an Aesthetica Creative Writing Award shortlist in poetry. In 2015 Exeter College at the University of Oxford awarded him a fully funded writing fellowship, an unusually competitive honor for a mid-career American writer. He is the author of seven books — Give Them Unquiet Dreams , Molly Bonamici , The Weight of Small Mercies , All We Ever Needed , Crossings , and companion volumes in publishing and craft — available on Amazon and through Silver Current Press. Since retiring from full-time teaching, he has directed his practice toward what he considers the most useful next act for a writer with his years and credentials: teaching adults to read literature and to write it, together, in the format that first made him love the work — the salon. He lives and works in Philadelphia. The courses in this catalog are the courses he most wants to teach and the ones he has been teaching, in one form or another, for years. title: A Note on My Philosophy of Writing · The 2601 Salon
heading: A Note on My Philosophy of Writing
description: A reflection on the imaginative and ethical commitments behind our gatherings, from James F. Mulhern.
text: A Note on My Philosophy of Writing · The 2601 Salon The 2601 Salon Courses About Thin Places Contact A Note on My Philosophy of Writing ✿ A reflection on the values behind our gatherings, from the salon's founder. I have never believed that any person, any longing, any grief, or any moment is truly new. There is nothing under the sun we have not felt before. Scripture said this first, and said it most plainly: “That which hath been is that which shall be, and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun” (Ecclesiastes 1:9). I did not arrive at this as a doctrine to be argued but as something I could not put down. I have spent a career of stories, poems, and two novels finding out how many ways it is true. I write as a Transcendentalist, in sensibility if not always in doctrine. Emerson taught me to trust the inner light and to call the great current beneath every separate life the Oversoul. Thoreau taught me to look long and closely at the near and the small until they open onto something larger—so closely that the aphorism a boy reads underlined in a dead man’s book ( “Goodness is the only investment that never fails” ) can, a generation later, save a stolen chalice from staying stolen. Whitman taught me that a single life, honestly told, contains multitudes and belongs to everyone who reads it. I am in their debt, and I have never tried to hide it. Hegel gives the same idea a different grammar. A thesis meets its antithesis; the two do not simply cancel one another but rise together into something neither could have been alone — sublated , in his word, which means canceled, preserved, and lifted up all at once. That is closer than “repetition” to what I mean when I say a scene, an image, or a grief returns in my work. It is not the same thing happening twice. It is the old thing and its opposite, meeting and carried forward, changed by the meeting. A theft becomes a return. A lie about leukemia becomes a real prayer said in the wrong pew. A ghost the world calls schizophrenia becomes, to the boy who sees it, an inheritance. Einstein supplies the physics for what Emerson, Hegel, and Ecclesiastes already knew in their own registers: that the distinction between past, present, and future is, in his own words, only a stubbornly persistent illusion. I take this as more than metaphor. I believe, as a matter of both faith and craft, that we are who we were, who we are, and who we will be, all at once, whether or not we have the instruments to measure it. In these stories, Laura—Aiden’s mother—knows this without needing the physics: she has seen her own mother caught in a pine tree years before she was born, and she recognizes the future when it arrives because it never stopped being present. I call this conviction, plainly, resurrection — not only the doctrine I was raised on, but the working premise of everything I write. What is loved and what is written does not end. It goes quiet for a while, and it comes back, changed. This is why the four stories in this book keep returning to the same rooms—why the reader will notice, and is meant to notice, certain scenes and images pass among them like family members moving from room to room. A grandmother who steals to protect the people she loves. A gold chalice taken from Mission Church and eventually returned to it. A cure sought in a psychiatric ward at McCall Hospital by way of a wine that ought not to be there. A blindfolded woman on a light-brown globe, playing a lyre with a single string, in a print called Hope —George Frederic Watts, 1886—that the mother has begun to copy in pencil. A star in the twilit sky above the hospital lawn, and, beneath it, a grandfather no one else can see. Yeats’s Innisfree, first as a poem pasted into a photo album and then as the boat in that album, and finally as a scarf caught on a branch—a small girl in a green pinafore, a small vision of a small girl in a green pinafore, one image folded inside the other. These recur across “Keep Calm and Carry On,” “The Wrong Way,” “Blindfolded,” and “Arise and Go Now” because I do not experience them as finished the first time I write them. They are simply where I return, the way a person returns to a family home long after the deed has changed hands. Read this way, the four stories in this book are, in one sense, one story told four times—from four angles, at four temperatures. A reader who resists that reading will still find four stories that, more strictly than most collections, share a family. The same conviction sends me both outward and inward. My fiction keeps company, often quietly, with writers who taught me to see. Yeats gave the boy a title, “Arise and Go Now,” and the mother her private landscape at Innisfree. Dickens loans Aiden a language for his father—a man like the Ghost of Christmas Past, going the wrong way in a snowstorm and unable to admit it. Hawthorne turns up in Rita’s kitchen with a warning about human frailty and sorrow. The nineteenth-century Watts hangs on Laura’s bed as a picture and, later, on the lawn of a mental hospital as a person. Even the doctrine of the venial and the mortal sin, argued over eggs and bacon, is a borrowing—from the Baltimore Catechism, from a whole immigrant Boston that taught its children where the line was and then, when love made it necessary, crossed it. This is pastiche in its oldest and most honest sense — not concealment, as plagiarism is, nor mockery, as parody can be, but homage: a debt acknowledged rather than hidden. I did not set out to prove I had read widely. I set out to show that admiration, followed far enough, becomes a form of collaboration across time — my sentences answering sentences finished long before I was born, the same way a later generation answers an earlier one without ever meeting it. None of this needs to be seen to be felt. A reader who notices none of it will still receive the whole of what any given story here intends — a family, a grief, a reckoning, a grace arrived at honestly. I have never wanted my work to require a key. But for the reader who happens to look twice, there is a second book folded quietly inside the first, in every book I have written. I have put it there on purpose, the way you might leave a light on in a room you don’t expect anyone to enter, just in case someone does. That second reader owes me nothing for the light. I only wanted it on. I understand this practice is easy to mislabel. In a writer, repetition is often read as a failure of invention, or worse, as a kind of theft from oneself. I do not experience it that way, and I do not think the record of my own work supports that reading. What returns in my writing is declared, not disguised — named outright when it matters, left as a private grace note when it does not, but never smuggled in on the assumption that no one would notice either way. When the chalice is stolen in one story and returned in the next, the reader is meant to see both movements. When the same twilit star appears above two hospital lawns, it is not carelessness. It is the point. I would rather a reader catch me returning to something than believe, wrongly, that I had run out of anything new to say. Recurrence, done honestly, is not the absence of invention. It is invention’s clearest proof: that a thing was worth making once and may be worth making again. A Sacred Thread What I have been describing, in Emerson’s language and in Hegel’s and in Einstein’s, comes down finally to a single conviction that runs, thread by thread, through every book I have written: that the living and the dead are joined, and that a life honestly told is a small opening onto that larger fabric. Emerson gave it the name I still find most useful, the Oversoul: the great current beneath every separate life. I do not mean this as decoration. I mean that the boy in Give Them Unquiet Dreams who sees his dead grandfather beneath a maple tree, and the boy in these Aiden stories who sees the same figure on a hospital lawn, are not two boys having the same hallucination. They are one boy, briefly permitted to see what is always there. Second sight, in my work, is not a supernatural gift. It is the ordinary human refusal to let the beloved dead be gone. The recurrences that mark my body of work follow from this belief. I return, again and again, to the same figures and the same rooms because I believe they are the same figures and the same rooms—that grief and grace, once entered into, do not stay behind. The Grandmother is the constant: Nana in these stories, Nana in Give Them Unquiet Dreams , the immigrant woman with the rosary and the cigarette and the ledger of small dishonesties committed on behalf of love. She is not a character I have deepened over the years so much as a presence I have learned to sit with longer. Behind her, half in shadow, stands the Grandfather—the drinker, the autodidact, the ghost on the lawn with the bottle-thick glasses, the one whose sentence about goodness saves a chalice a generation later. The Mother is broken and luminous: her second sight named as illness by the doctors, honored as inheritance by the child. The Father is the one going the wrong way in the snow, unable to admit it. The Boy—Aiden, Josh, whatever name I have given him—is the one who has been asked, too early, to hold the family up, and who does, and who pays for it. The scenes recur as well, and I mean for them to. The stolen sacred object—a chalice, a rosary, a set of keys—returned or restored. The kitchen table where a lie is told for someone’s protection and, at the same table, later, a prayer. The hospital corridor, its ordinary institutional cruelties softened by the odd holy figure a nurse or aide turns out to be. The car ride home in silence after everything has changed. The window at dawn, someone at it, someone gone. The twilit star. Yeats’s bee-loud glade, first as a poem, then as a boat, then as a real body of water a woman remembers she once lived beside. The blindfolded figure on the light-brown globe, playing a lyre with a single string, in a print called Hope . A snowfall that both hides and reveals. A watch stopped at 1:03. These are not motifs I chose out of a workshop drawer. They are the furniture of the house I have been living in as a writer, and I move them from novel to poem to story the way any person moves the good chair from one room to another when the light changes. The conflicts recur, too, because they are the conflicts I know. Faith against psychiatry: the Catholic child’s knowledge that his mother is not sick but visited, running up against the doctor’s knowledge that she is not visited but sick. Both parties love the woman; both are, in their own light, right; the story survives by refusing to choose. Loyalty against law: the grandmother who steals what she cannot afford in order to keep the family fed and clothed and, once, cured. Duty against departure: the boy who wants a life of his own and the boy who cannot leave a grandmother at the kitchen window. Silence against confession: the immigrant reticence of not telling what happened, and the American compulsion to tell everything. These are not, I think, my private conflicts. They are the conflicts of Irish-American Catholic life in the second half of the twentieth century, and they belong to more people than have yet written them down. I have written this ending, in different rooms and with different windows, more than once. The clearest version I have yet managed is the closing pages of Give Them Unquiet Dreams , and I would rather quote them here than restate them: In every beginning is an ending, and in every ending is a beginning. There is no time between, only eternity. When we pass on, we move into another room. Our departed loved ones are a short distance away—in that room just beyond the doorway. They lean in softly, watching over us, taking turns to check that we are safe, placing unseen palms upon our hearts, whispering loveliness in our ears. They are joyful in our joy. They are sad in our sadness. They laugh as we laugh. And they tell stories. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” In the other room right now, in this eternal moment, Martin is talking with Grandpa. My father is talking with my mother. And my grandmother is chatting too. Nearby, a line of people stretches backward to the moment of Creation. A symphony of voices, murmurs, and inflections, mingling hands and mingling glances, observing the past, the present, and the future. In this time, at the same time, and for all time. That is what I believe, and I would rather say it there, in a scene, than defend it here in an argument. Still, I want to name it plainly. The living and the dead are one people, united by love, which does not observe the border we imagine between them. Love is an eternal presence, and it moves in both directions—forward toward the ones not yet arrived, and backward, no less real, toward the ones we say have gone. All life is resurrection. Every experience we have had returns in another, subtly changed—a grandmother’s hand at the back of a grandson’s neck becoming, a generation later, that grandson’s hand at the back of his own son’s; a mother’s fingers tracing the shape of a face becoming, without warning, the same tracing at another bedside, decades on, in another light. No person is ever lost. We are their resurrections. We relive their lives in transfiguration—altered, and altered again—and paradoxically imbued, in every alteration, with a great sameness that is not repetition but recognition, the sameness of a single spark passing through many lanterns. In this time, in all time, and eternally. And because all time, in the end, is the same time, we are one people: not divided into the living and the dead, but united by a single essential spark that illuminates, in each of us for a little while, the consciousness of the Oversoul: hallowed, and whole. To write, for me, has been to sit close enough to that spark to feel its heat, and to record honestly the small ordinary rooms in which it becomes briefly visible—a kitchen, a hospital corridor, a snowbound car heading, as fathers do, the wrong way home. My debts, in all this, are declared rather than smuggled. Yeats gave me the bee-loud glade and the title “Arise and Go Now.” Joyce gave me the last paragraph of “The Dead,” which I have been trying, in my honest moments, to answer for thirty years—the snow “general all over Ireland,” falling on the living and the dead alike, because they are one country. Dickens gave me the Ghost of Christmas Past, going the wrong way in a snowstorm. Emily Dickinson gave me the permission to end on a hyphen. Flannery O’Connor gave me grace as ambush. Emerson gave me the Oversoul. Thoreau gave me the sentence underlined in a dead man’s book. Whitman gave me the confidence that one small immigrant kitchen in Boston could contain, if I looked at it long enough, everyone I would ever meet or lose. I would rather a reader hear those voices moving underneath mine than not hear them. My work is not an argument for originality. It is an argument for company—across the border between the living and the dead, and across the border between one writer’s book and another’s. Beneath the theology and the theory, though, lies something plainer, and I want to end there rather than in abstraction. Long before I had read Emerson or Hegel, or understood what Einstein believed about time, I had a grandmother named Helen, who prayed to the Blessed Mother before anyone else, loved me by whatever means were available to her, honest and otherwise, and has never, in any real sense I can measure, left my work. Every grandmother in every book I have written is, in some flawed and partial way, a return to her. Catherine, in these stories—Nana—is one such return: not Helen, and not a portrait of Helen, but the same current running through a different vessel, honest about its dishonesties, tender in the shape her tenderness could take. I did not need a philosophy to justify that. I needed one only later, to explain it to myself. Everything else — the guides, the snow, the borrowed names, the verses pasted onto the backs of old photographs — is what I found once I went looking for the shape of what I already believed: that nothing we love is ever finished happening. It only goes quiet, waits to be carried forward, and rises again, a little changed, in someone else’s hands, or in mine, one more time. — James Mulhern — James F. title: Thin Places · The 2601 Salon
heading: Thin Places
description: What my friend Carol knew about permeable membranes, long before anyone put it in a study — an essay by James Mulhern.
text: Thin Places · The 2601 Salon The 2601 Salon For Partners Table of Contents Courses Formats Philosophy Enroll or Book An Essay Thin Places ✿ What my friend Carol knew about permeable membranes, long before anyone put it in a study. I. A Phrase My Grandmother Would Have Known There is an old phrase from the Ireland my grandmother came out of: a thin place . It names a spot on the earth where the wall between this world and the next has worn thin — a holy well, a ruin, a stretch of shore at a certain hour of the evening. Nobody who used the phrase meant it as a figure of speech. They meant it plainly. Some ground is more permeable than other ground, and if you stand on it, you should expect company. I have come to believe that some people are thin places too. Not haunted, not troubled — just built with less wall between one thing and another. And once you see it in yourself, you start noticing it everywhere: in the friend who cries at other people’s weddings, in the child who asks a hundred questions a day, in the artist who can’t quite tell you where the idea came from because it arrived already finished, feeling like a memory rather than an invention. This is an essay about that kind of person. I am one of them. And I want to tell you about the woman who named it for me before I had any language for it at all. II. Carol When I was a boy, I asked questions. Not the ordinary kind children ask and then forget. I asked and asked, circled back, asked again, chased an idea down five more corridors before I let it go — if I ever let it go. I found the world of the imagined every bit as real, sometimes more real, than the world in front of me. Grown-ups found this tiring. Other children found it strange. I found it, mostly, embarrassing. Carol didn’t. Carol was a former nun who had gone on to become a psychologist, and for reasons I still don’t fully understand, she took an interest in a curious, chattering boy who talked too much and imagined too hard. She became my mentor and, in time, one of the people I loved most in this world. One day, worn down by my own barrage of questions, feeling the familiar sting of having been too much again, I must have looked at her the way children look when they expect to be told to quiet down. Instead she smiled and said, “Jimmy, you ask so many questions because you have permeable membranes.” I didn’t know what the words meant. I only knew what her face meant. She wasn’t correcting me. She was naming something in me and telling me, in the same breath, that it was all right to have it. The shame I’d been carrying — the sense that my curiosity was a nuisance, a defect, something to apologize for — loosened its grip a little that day, and has been loosening ever since. It took me until adulthood to understand how unnecessary that shame had been in the first place. Carol saw that decades before I did. Carol has passed now — moved on, as I think of it, to the other room. But I have carried her sentence with me for most of my life without ever finding out where it came from or whether it was true in any way beyond her own kindness and her own good instincts. Then, not long ago, I came across the work of a psychiatrist named Ernest Hartmann, and I sat up in my chair, because there it was: permeable membranes, decades later, with a name and a body of research behind it. III. What Hartmann Found Hartmann spent years studying people who suffered from frequent nightmares, and he noticed something curious about them. Their trouble wasn’t only that their dreams were bad. It was that the walls inside their minds, generally, seemed to be thinner than other people’s walls — not just around sleep, but around almost everything: the line between thought and feeling, between self and other, between the past and the present, between the fanciful and the real. So he built a way of measuring it. He asked people a long series of questions about how they experience the world — whether they can focus on one thing while shutting everything else out, whether they know for certain when they’re awake and when they’re dreaming, whether an idea ever arrives to them already wrapped in a feeling, whether they think of people and situations in clean categories or in shades that blur into one another. What he found was a real, measurable range of human temperament, running from thick to thin. At the thick end sits a person with sharp, well-kept boundaries. Thought stays separate from feeling. Sleep and waking are two distinct rooms with a closed door between them. The past is filed and finished. People and ideas sort easily into categories: this and not that, us and them. At the thin end sits someone quite different. Sensation and idea pour in together, all at once, and sorting it into tidy piles is hard work. A thought rarely shows up alone — it comes trailing a feeling, the way Carol’s sentence came trailing a smile I still remember decades later. The border between waking and dreaming is soft; such a person drifts easily into daydream and has trouble finding the door back out. The past does not stay past — it visits, uninvited and vivid, blended right into the present moment. And the line between what is real and what is imagined can, at times, go faint enough that the imagined feels every bit as urgent as the real. Hartmann called this trait boundary thinness, and what struck me most, reading his work, was not the theory. It was the recognition. I knew this person. I had been this person my whole life, and someone had told me so, gently, when I was still young enough to need the telling. IV. Thin Boundaries and the Inner Life People with thinner boundaries, Hartmann discovered, tend to have more vivid dreams and remember them more often. They are more prone to nightmares, yes — but also to something better than nightmares: what researchers call episodes of total absorption. Moments when a book, a piece of music, a memory, or an idea seizes the whole of a person’s attention so completely that the outside world simply falls away. Time changes shape. Distraction becomes impossible. And, strangely, the thing being attended to starts to feel more real, not less, than ordinary life. Some people with especially thin boundaries live much of their waking life inside a rich, private, internal world — one so vivid that it can feel, briefly, indistinguishable from the world everyone else is standing in. I recognized every bit of this. I was the boy who found an imagined conversation more compelling than the real one happening in the room, who could vanish into a story or a daydream so thoroughly that someone had to say my name twice to bring me back. I did not think of this as unusual until other people told me, in one way or another, that it was. Carol was the only person who ever told me it was unusual and good. And here is the detail that stopped me cold when I first read it: Hartmann found that art and music students scored, on average, thinner than the general population. The very trait that made me an inconvenient child at the dinner table — too many questions, too much imagination, too little patience for the literal — turns out to be more common among the people who spend their lives making things. V. The Poets Already Knew Here is what surprised me most as I sat with all this. Hartmann was not the first to notice any of it. Poets had been describing the very same thing two hundred years earlier — they simply didn’t have a clinical name for it. John Keats, writing to his brothers when he was twenty-two, tried to describe what made Shakespeare Shakespeare. He landed on a phrase he called Negative Capability — the ability to sit inside uncertainty and doubt without grasping after a tidy answer. That is a thick-boundaried person’s nightmare and a thin-boundaried person’s native climate. Keats went further in another letter, saying the poet “has no self,” that he can pour himself into a sparrow outside the window and peck about in the gravel right along with it. Read that today and it sounds like someone describing, four generations before the questionnaire existed, exactly what it feels like to have very little wall between yourself and the rest of the world. Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Keats’s older contemporary, coined a strange word for the same thing: esemplastic, meaning “shaped into one.” He used it to describe the imagination’s power to dissolve separate things and melt them into a single new thing. That is not so different from what happens when a memory and a present moment blend together without asking permission, or when a feeling arrives to you already wearing the shape of a physical object — a cracked heel, a broken piano, a streetlight that is too bright. The Romantics called this imagination. Hartmann, without ever having read a line of Coleridge as far as I know, ended up measuring the same thing with a questionnaire. And then there is William Wordsworth, who wrote that we come into the world “trailing clouds of glory,” and that childhood is soaked in a kind of visionary brightness most of us lose as we grow older. He asked, achingly, “Whither is fled the visionary gleam?” For two centuries readers took that as a poem about the sadness of growing up. But it reads differently once you know that thin boundaries, on average, do thicken with age — that most people’s walls harden as they mature, while a smaller number of people keep something of that early permeability their whole lives. Wordsworth was not just being wistful. He may have been describing something real: most people lose the gleam, and a few simply don’t. I find this enormously comforting. It means Carol and Hartmann and Keats and Wordsworth were all, in their own centuries and their own languages, pointing at the same small miracle: some people keep more of childhood’s brightness than others, and that is not a flaw to grow out of. It may be the very thing that makes a person a writer, a painter, a musician — or just someone who never stopped asking questions at the dinner table. VI. A Question Worth Asking This is what I keep circling back to, and the question this essay wants to leave you with rather than answer completely: is there a real connection between thin boundaries and creativity? I don’t think the connection is an accident, and I don’t think it’s flattering in a simple way, either. A person with thin boundaries is, almost by definition, someone for whom things blend that other people keep separate — memory and imagination, feeling and thought, the dead and the living, the self and the person across the table. That blending is exhausting. It is also, I suspect, very close to the raw material of art. You cannot write a character from the inside, or make a metaphor that actually surprises someone, or paint a color that feels like grief, unless something in you is willing to let the borders go soft for a while. Carol didn’t need a questionnaire to see this in me. She just watched a boy ask too many questions and understood, faster than I ever could have, what that habit was actually made of. She gave me the gift of a name for something I had only ever experienced as a flaw. It took Hartmann’s research, decades later, to tell me she had been right all along — and to suggest that what she saw in me might be worth more than either of us knew. I no longer feel any embarrassment about my permeable membranes. I think of them now the way Carol seemed to, all those years ago: not as a defect to manage, but as a kind of instrument — one that happens to be a little more finely strung than most, and that, if you let it, will pick up sounds other people miss entirely. — James Mulhern — James F. title: Our Building, Our Story: Writing the Life of 2601 · The 2601 Salon
heading: Our Building, Our Story: Writing the Life of 2601
description: A ten-session personal essay course for the residents of 2601 — craft fundamentals, the ethics of writing about real people, and five essay forms (arrival, portrait, joy, hardship, comedy, and the unforgettable) that build toward a shared, publishable resident anthology. Taught by James F. Mulhern.

See the partners page or download a one-page flyer for this course . Notices & Announcements Posted Current Welcome to The 2601 Salon — a working catalog of literary courses for adult readers and writers, offered in person or on Zoom. To learn more, express interest, or bring a course to your venue, email Professor Mulhern at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . The Whiteboard is available on every course page for live in-class notes. Our Building, Our Story: Writing the Life of 2601 Ten Sessions A literary course for adult readers and writers · taught by James F. Mulhern ‹ Back to all courses What would you like to see? Click any button below. Important Information & Course Materials ▾ An Invitation ▾ Every building is a village. Behind each door on every floor at 2601 is a life — an arrival story, a triumph, a private sorrow, a friendship struck up in the elevator, a joke that is still funny fifteen years later. Most of it is never written down. It lives only in conversation, and then, eventually, it doesn’t live anywhere at all. This course exists to change that. Over ten sessions, the residents of 2601 will learn to write the personal essay — clearly, honestly, and well — and will use those new skills to build a shared book: a collection of true, first-person essays about what it has meant to live in this particular building, among these particular neighbors, in this particular slice of a life. No experience is required. No one needs to have written anything since a high school assignment. You only need a memory, a willingness to look at it honestly, and ninety minutes a week. By the end, we will have a manuscript — a real one, ready for the kind of independent publication available to any of us through print-on-demand services such as Amazon KDP. A book with your neighbors’ names on the spine, on the shelf, in the lobby, and in your own hands. Welcome ▾ Welcome to Our Building, Our Story — a ten-session course in personal essay writing, built specifically for the residents of 2601 and organized around a single shared subject: this building, and your life within it. The first four sessions teach the craft fundamentals every essayist needs — brainstorming, structuring an essay, drafting a scene, and revising with a clear eye — using 2601 itself as the shared material for every exercise. The next five sessions each introduce one essay type particular to a residential community: the arrival story, the neighbor portrait, the happy memory, the hard memory, the funniest memory, and the most unforgettable moment. The final session is a workshop and manuscript-planning meeting, where the group decides, together, how the individual essays will become one collective book. This is not a memoir-writing marathon. Each essay is short — the kind of piece a person can draft in one sitting and refine in two or three more. The goal is a body of work every contributor can be proud of, gathered into something permanent. I am glad to be teaching this course, and I am glad you are here. What This Course Is ▾ This is a beginner-friendly workshop in the personal essay, using the shared experience of living at 2601 as its subject matter throughout. Each week we will: Learn one specific craft skill (brainstorming, outlining, scene-writing, revision, or a particular essay form) See that skill demonstrated with short published examples Practice the skill directly on 2601 material, in class, by hand or by laptop Leave with a clear, short take-home assignment: a complete draft of that week’s essay By Session 10, every participant will have a folder of five to seven short personal essays, each between 500 and 1,200 words, all set at or shaped by 2601 — ready to be assembled, edited, and published as a shared building anthology. What This Course Is Not ▾ It is not a gossip session. We write about our own experience of people and events — not to expose, wound, or settle scores. It is not a legal risk. Session 4 is devoted entirely to writing about real people and real events without inviting a lawsuit — a subject every contributor must take seriously before anyone’s essay is considered for the shared book. It is not mandatory disclosure. You choose what to write about. No one will ask you to reveal more than you want to. It is not a contest. There will be no ranking of essays. Every finished, honest piece belongs in the anthology if its author wants it there. It is not a one-way lecture. Bring your stories. The best material in this course will come from you, not from me. About the Instructor ▾ James F. Mulhern is a Professor of English and a former Department Chair, and the recipient of a fully funded Writing Fellowship at Exeter College, University of Oxford. He is a published author whose short fiction, essays, and poetry have appeared in more than 350 literary journals, and he is the founder of Silver Current Press. He has taught writing at the university level for many years and has a particular, long-standing interest in the way ordinary communities — families, workplaces, neighborhoods, buildings — hold literature inside them that no one has yet written down. He lives at 2601. Course Details ▾ Course Title Our Building, Our Story: Writing the Life of 2601 Instructor James F. Mulhern Format In person, in a common room or lounge at 2601 Duration Ten weeks Session Length Ninety minutes Cost Offered free to residents of 2601 Class Size Open to all residents Materials Notebook or laptop; a copy of the companion text (see below) is recommended but not required Grading None End Product A shared, print-ready manuscript of resident essays, suitable for self-publication A Recommended Companion Text ▾ For residents who would like a book to read alongside the course, I recommend: Bill Roorbach with Kristen Keckler, Writing Life Stories: How to Make Memories into Memoirs, Ideas into Essays, and Life into Literature (Tenth Anniversary Edition, Writer’s Digest Books). This book is the single best-suited guide I know for a group exactly like ours: working writers and non-writers alike, drawing directly on lived memory, with no academic jargon and no assumption of prior training. Roorbach’s chapters on finding material, building scenes from memory, and shaping a true story into a finished essay map closely onto what we will do together, week by week. It is widely available secondhand and at public libraries, and no purchase is required to succeed in this course — I will bring copies to class, and every technique in the book is also taught directly in these session materials. An alternate, equally strong choice for anyone who wants a second opinion on the craft: Dinty W. Moore, Crafting the Personal Essay: A Guide for Writing and Publishing Creative Nonfiction (Writer’s Digest Books), which is especially good on classifying essay types and on the practical mechanics of turning a finished draft into something ready to submit or publish. Schedule at a Glance ▾ Session Focus 1 Welcome & Brainstorming — finding your 2601 material 2 Outlining & Planning — giving a true story a shape 3 Scene, Voice, and the First Draft — putting the reader in the room 4 Writing About Real People Without a Lawsuit — the ethics and law of the personal essay 5 The Arrival Essay — how and why you came to 2601 6 The Neighbor Portrait — someone who marked your time here 7 The Happy Memory — joy, in scene 8 The Hard Memory — writing loss, conflict, and difficulty with care 9 The Funniest Experience at 2601 — writing comedy that is also true 10 The Most Unforgettable Experience & Workshop — final essay, revision, and building the shared manuscript Glossary ▾ Brainstorming An unfiltered, quantity-first method of generating raw material for writing, in which the writer lists memories, images, or ideas without editing or judging them. Sorting and selection happen only after the list exists. Situation / Turn / Insight A simple three-part shape for a personal essay: the situation (what things were like before), the turn (what happened or changed), and the insight (what the writer now understands as a result). Nearly every short personal essay can be mapped onto this structure. Scene A moment of narrative rendered in close, sensory detail — as opposed to summary, which covers time and events more quickly and generally. Scene puts the reader inside a specific moment. Voice The distinct, recognizable personality that comes through a writer’s specific word choices, rhythm, and way of noticing the world. In personal essay, voice should sound like an honest, particular person — not a generic “writerly” tone. Defamation A false statement of fact, presented as fact rather than opinion, that damages a real person’s reputation. Personal essays that stick to the writer’s own experience and clearly-framed opinions carry far less legal risk than essays that assert unverifiable claims about another person’s character or actions. Invasion of Privacy / Public Disclosure of Private Facts A legal concern distinct from defamation: even a true statement about someone can expose a writer to liability if it discloses a highly private fact (medical, financial, or similarly sensitive) that the subject had a reasonable expectation would remain private, and the disclosure would be considered highly offensive to a reasonable person. Anthology A collected volume of writing by multiple authors, gathered around a shared theme. The finished product of this course is a resident-written anthology: a single published book containing every contributor’s finished essays. Print-on-Demand (POD) Publishing A publishing model, of which Amazon KDP is the most widely used example, in which a book is printed one copy at a time as orders arrive, rather than in a large advance print run. This makes small, community-scale books like a building anthology financially practical to publish. Reading Companion Essay ▾ Why a Building Deserves a Book Every apartment building accumulates a kind of oral history that almost never survives its residents. Someone remembers the year the boiler failed in January. Someone remembers the doorman who knew every child’s name on the block. Someone remembers exactly how the light came through the lobby windows on the day they first walked in, hopeful and a little frightened, carrying a single box because the movers hadn’t come yet. And then, eventually — because people move, because people age, because people pass away — all of it is gone, the way almost everything about almost everyone is eventually gone, unless someone writes it down. This is not a small loss. A building like 2601 is not merely an address; it is a sustained, ongoing act of communal life — hundreds of small kindnesses, hundreds of small frictions, celebrations and losses experienced in close physical proximity to people who did not choose each other, exactly, but who ended up choosing, in whatever way, to stay. That is worth a book. The personal essay is the right form for this project because it does not require its writers to have any particular credential or life story. It asks only for honesty and attention. You do not need to have done anything remarkable to write a remarkable essay about living here — you need only to look closely at what actually happened, choose the moments that matter, and render them so a stranger could feel them too. What you are being asked to do in this course, session by session, is what every essayist has always done: to take the enormous, undifferentiated material of a lived life and select from it — deliberately, carefully, sometimes painfully — the handful of moments that carry the most truth. Brainstorming finds the material. Outlining gives it shape. Scene-writing makes it vivid. The session on writing about real people keeps it safe and fair. And the five essay types that follow — arrival, portrait, joy, hardship, comedy, and the most unforgettable experience of all — simply point that same set of tools at the different rooms of a life lived at 2601. By the end, you will not just have learned to write personal essays. You will have helped build something that did not exist before: a permanent, physical record of what it meant to live, for however many years, in this particular building, among these particular people, at this particular moment. Long after any of us are still here, someone — a future resident, a grown child of a current one, a stranger who buys the book secondhand — will be able to open it and know, in specific and vivid detail, what it was like. That is not a small thing to have made. It is, in fact, a form of care for the people who will come after you, the truest kind a writer can offer: I was here. I paid attention. Here is what it was like. About Me ▾ I am a Professor of English and a former Department Chair, and I am the recipient of a fully funded Writing Fellowship at Exeter College, University of Oxford. My own short fiction, essays, and poetry have appeared in more than 350 literary journals, and I am the founder of Silver Current Press, an independent publishing house. I have taught writing at the university level for most of my adult life. I also live at 2601, which is why this course exists. I have my own arrival story, my own portraits of neighbors I have loved, my own hard memories and my own very funny ones — and I believe, without reservation, that every one of my neighbors has at least one essay in them worth reading, and that together, we have a book worth making. If you have questions, or want to talk about an essay you are already working on, please email me at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . This course is offered free of charge to the residents of 2601. All materials are for educational use within the course, in service of the shared resident anthology it is designed to produce. About the Use of These Materials ▾ These materials — course descriptions, reading lists, syllabi, discussion questions, session pages, and prompts — were written and designed by James F. Mulhern for Silver Current Press. Readers are welcome to read, print, share, and quote them for personal use and study. Teachers, program directors, and institutions who would like to use any of this material in a classroom, syllabus, publication, or paid program are asked to write first — a short email is enough. The answer will almost always be a warm yes, with a note on attribution. Please contact Professor Mulhern at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . The Sessions ▾ Session 1 — Welcome & Brainstorming: Finding Your 2601 Material Session 2 — Outlining & Planning: Giving a True Story a Shape Session 3 — Scene, Voice, and the First Draft: Putting the Reader in the Room Session 4 — Writing About Real People Without a Lawsuit: The Ethics and Law of the Personal Essay Session 5 — The Arrival Essay: How and Why You Came to 2601 Session 6 — The Neighbor Portrait: Someone Who Marked Your Time Here Session 7 — The Happy Memory: Joy, in Scene Session 8 — The Hard Memory: Writing Loss, Conflict, and Difficulty With Care Session 9 — The Funniest Experience at 2601: Writing Comedy That Is Also True Session 10 — The Most Unforgettable Experience & Workshop: Final Essay, Revision, and Building the Shared Manuscript ‹ Close Session 1 — Welcome & Brainstorming: Finding Your 2601 Material Main Points of the Lesson Everyone in this room already has enough material for ten essays. The problem beginning writers face is almost never a shortage of experience — it is not yet knowing how to find it, sort it, and recognize which memories are actually alive. Brainstorming is the tool that solves this. Brainstorming works by lowering the bar, not raising it. The goal in the first pass is quantity, not quality. Write down every memory of the building that surfaces, no matter how small, boring, or unfinished it seems. Sorting happens later. Specific beats general every time. “I’ve lived here a long time and made good friends” is not yet an essay. “The night the power went out on the ninth floor and Mrs. Alvarez knocked on every door with a flashlight and a deck of cards” is the beginning of one. Specificity is the whole craft in miniature. A good brainstorming list has categories. For this course, useful categories include: arrivals and departures, neighbors, doormen and staff, holidays and building events, small emergencies, the view, the elevator, the lobby, noise, weather, pets, children growing up in the building, losses, celebrations, and anything that made you laugh. The senses unlock memory faster than thinking does. Before you try to remember what happened, try to remember what you smelled, heard, or touched. The smell of a hallway, the sound of a particular door, the temperature of the lobby in winter — these sensory details are often the door back into a fuller memory. In-Class Practice Fifteen minutes. On a blank page, write “2601” at the top and then, without stopping to judge or polish, list every memory, image, or person connected to the building that comes to mind. Aim for at least twenty items — some can be a single word (“elevator,” “Mrs. Alvarez,” “moving day,” “the blackout”). Do not write full sentences yet. Just make the list as long as possible. Discussion Questions Look at your list. Which three items make you feel something the moment you write them down — a small jolt of feeling, whether warm or uncomfortable? Those are usually the strongest material. Is there an item on your list you’re surprised you remembered? Why do you think it surfaced? What is the very first memory you have of 2601 — the earliest one, from your first days here? Where does it rank on your list? Which category (arrivals, neighbors, building events, small emergencies, and so on) produced the most items for you? What does that tell you about what you notice and remember? Is there anything on your list you are hesitant to write about? You do not have to explain why — just notice it. We will return to that question in Session 4. Homework Circle the five strongest items on your brainstorm list. For each one, write one sentence that is as specific and concrete as you can make it — not “a funny thing happened with my neighbor,” but “Mr. Petrosky once brought his goldfish to the lobby in a soup pot during a fire drill.” Bring all five sentences to Session 2. ‹ Close Session 2 — Outlining & Planning: Giving a True Story a Shape Main Points of the Lesson A true story is not yet an essay until it has a shape. Life does not arrive in essay form. The writer’s job is to select a beginning, middle, and end from the much longer, messier reality of what actually happened — and that selection is an act of design, not falsification. The simplest reliable shape is: situation, turn, insight. Begin with where things stood. Introduce a turn — something changed, arrived, was said, or was lost. End with what you now understand that you did not understand before it happened. This three-part shape underlies almost every successful short personal essay. An outline is a promise you make to your reader, then keep. Before drafting, jot four or five lines describing what happens in order. This is not a straitjacket — you can and should deviate once you start writing — but it prevents the wandering, directionless draft that beginning writers most often produce. Choose your ending before you choose your opening. Knowing where an essay is going to land — what realization or image will close it — makes every earlier decision easier. Many writers draft the last line or last image first, then build backward toward it. Cut everything that does not serve the shape you have chosen. An outline also tells you what to leave out.
