heading: Survey of American Literature
description: A sixteen-session course in American literature, taught by James F. Mulhern — open to adult readers, offered in person or online.
text: Survey of American Literature · The 2601 Salon The 2601 Salon For Partners Table of Contents Courses Formats Philosophy Thin Places Enroll or Book For program partners: This course can be brought to any adult reading audience — in person or on Zoom. See the partners page or download a one-page flyer for this course . Notices & Announcements Posted Current Welcome to The 2601 Salon — a working catalog of literary courses for adult readers and writers, offered in person or on Zoom. To learn more, express interest, or bring a course to your venue, email Professor Mulhern at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . The Whiteboard is available on every course page for live in-class notes. Survey of American Literature Sixteen Sessions A literary course for adult readers and writers · taught by James F. Mulhern ‹ Back to all courses What would you like to see? Click any button below. Important Information & Course Materials ▾ An Invitation ▾ You live in a city that was there at the beginning of this country’s story. Philadelphia is in the literature — in the pamphlets of Benjamin Franklin, in the oratory of Frederick Douglass, in the jazz-soaked streets that Langston Hughes knew. You do not have to go anywhere to find America’s literary past. Some of it happened a few blocks from where you are sitting right now. This course is an invitation to read it together — slowly, attentively, and without any pressure to sound like you have a degree in anything. Literature is not a closed room. It is a conversation that began before any of us arrived, and it goes on as long as we are willing to keep talking. I have been teaching literature for more than three decades. I believe strongly in one thing: the best discussions happen between equals. You bring your experience, your questions, your willingness to be surprised. I will bring the books and a few good questions. After that, the course takes care of itself. Come as you are. Welcome ▾ If you have opened this page, you are already the kind of person this course is for. You are curious. You have noticed that good writing does something to you — slows you down, or speeds your pulse, or makes you feel less alone — and you want to understand why. This is a non-graded, discussion-based course meeting once a week in the room. It asks nothing of you except a willingness to read a modest amount beforehand and to say what you think once you get here. There are no quizzes, no papers, no grades. Nothing said in this room is repeated outside it. You may not agree with your fellow readers, and I hope you do not always agree with me. Over sixteen weeks we will move through American literature from its earliest surviving voices to writers working in our own era. We will read poems, short stories, essays, speeches, and — if the group is willing — one longer work together. Every text we read is either in the public domain or available free through a linked public source; all links are provided below. What This Course Is ▾ A chronological survey of American literature, organized by period and theme, from pre-colonial oral traditions through contemporary voices. Each major period receives two sessions — enough time to read carefully, change our minds, and follow a question further than a single meeting allows. Discussion is the center of every class. We read closely, think carefully, disagree respectfully, and follow the conversation wherever it leads. This is also a course about Philadelphia. We live in a city that appears, directly or by implication, in the story of American literature at nearly every turn. I will point those connections out as they arise. What This Course Is Not ▾ This is not a lecture course. I will frame the period at the start of each session — perhaps fifteen minutes — and after that, the room belongs to you. It is not a course that requires prior literary study. If you have never read a poem for pleasure, this is a perfectly good place to start. If you have read widely, you will find things here that are new to you. It is not a course designed to arrive at a single correct interpretation. American literature is contested ground — about who counts as American, whose voice gets recorded, whose story gets told. We will sit with that discomfort rather than resolve it too quickly. There are no wrong answers. There are only answers you cannot yet support. Syllabus ▾ Session Period Focus 1 Pre-Colonial Indigenous voices — oral tradition, cosmology, the land 2 Colonial & Puritan Bradford, Winthrop, Edwards — the errand into the wilderness 3 Enlightenment & Early Republic Jefferson, Franklin — the rhetoric of liberty 4 Slavery & the Counter-Narrative Equiano, Wheatley — who is excluded from “all men”? 5 Romanticism & Transcendentalism Emerson, Thoreau — the self against the world 6 The American Gothic Hawthorne, Poe — sin, guilt, the uncanny 7 Civil War & Reconstruction I Douglass, Lincoln — the reckoning in prose 8 Civil War & Reconstruction II Whitman, Dickinson — the reckoning in poetry 9 Realism & Naturalism I Gilman, Chopin — confinement and the women who named it 10 Realism & Naturalism II Dunbar, Chesnutt — race and the performance of survival 11 Modernism I Frost, Robinson — the spoken voice, the dark undertow 12 Modernism II Williams, H.D., Sandburg — image, city, the new American line 13 Harlem Renaissance I McKay, Hughes — defiance and the dream 14 Harlem Renaissance II Hurston, Toomer — joy, folk voice, the interior life 15 Mid-Century & Civil Rights Plath, Sexton, King — the private made public 16 Contemporary Voices & Capstone Cisneros, Komunyakaa, Harjo — here, now, and where we began Optional anchor text (the group votes in Session 1): - The Crucible by Arthur Miller — seventeenth-century setting, mid-century political fear, easy to read aloud; pair with Sessions 2 and 6 - The Scarlet Letter by Nathaniel Hawthorne — rich for sin, shame, and gender; expand Session 6 to two sessions on this novel - To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee — narrative accessibility, race and justice; pair with Sessions 9–10, noting its limitations candidly The Scarlet Letter is in the public domain — Project Gutenberg . For The Crucible and To Kill a Mockingbird , free borrows are available via Internet Archive (search by title). Instructor will also distribute excerpts as needed. Course Details ▾ Title: Survey of American Literature Instructor: James F. Mulhern, Professor of English; former Department Chair; Writing Fellow, Exeter College, University of Oxford Format: In person or on Zoom Schedule: Weekly, 90 minutes Cost: Contact for current terms Credits: None Grading: None Prerequisites: None What to Expect Each Week ▾ Each session follows a consistent shape: Historical frame (10–15 min) — I will place the period in brief context: what was happening politically, socially, and artistically when these texts were written. Close reading (15–20 min) — We read a short passage aloud together. Someone volunteers; no one is called on. Guided discussion (45–50 min) — Four to six questions, written in advance, offered to the room. The conversation goes where it needs to go. In-class practice (10 min) — A short writing or reflection exercise, entirely optional. You may listen while others write. Optional writing prompt — Offered at the end; something to carry home if you want it. Readings for each session are short — typically one to three poems, a brief essay, or a story of fifteen pages or fewer. Everything is linked below. A Few Promises to You ▾ I will not call on you. I will not ask you to read aloud unless you volunteer. I will not embarrass you, correct you publicly, or tell you that your reading of a text is wrong. I will be prepared. The historical frame will be tight and useful, not a lecture that wanders. I will bring my honest opinion, and I will tell you when I am uncertain. This course will end on time. A Few Asks of You ▾ Read the assigned texts before class, even if only once. Come with at least one thing you noticed — a line, an image, a question. Give your fellow readers the same generosity you would want in return. Disagree out loud. Polite silence is the enemy of a good seminar. Leave your phone in your pocket. Schedule at a Glance ▾ Session Title Key Authors 1 The First Voices Iroquois, Ojibwe, Cherokee 2 The Errand into the Wilderness Bradford, Winthrop, Edwards 3 The Language of Liberty Jefferson, Franklin, Paine 4 The Counter-Narrative Equiano, Wheatley 5 The Self in Nature Emerson, Thoreau, Irving 6 The American Gothic Hawthorne, Poe 7 War, Justice, and Prose Douglass, Lincoln 8 War, Mourning, and Poetry Whitman, Dickinson 9 Confinement and Its Names Gilman, Chopin 10 The Mask and the Story Dunbar, Chesnutt 11 The Voice in the Wall Frost, Robinson 12 The Image on the Street Williams, Sandburg, H.D. 13 Defiance and the Dream McKay, Hughes 14 Joy, Folk, and the Interior Hurston, Toomer 15 The Private Made Public Plath, Sexton, King 16 Here, Now — Capstone Cisneros, Komunyakaa, Harjo Literary Terms Glossary ▾ Allegory — A narrative in which characters, settings, and events stand for abstract ideas or moral qualities. Hawthorne’s veil is an allegory for hidden sin. Bildungsroman — A novel of formation or coming-of-age. The House on Mango Street is a compressed, lyrical example. Close reading — The practice of reading a text slowly and carefully, attending to word choice, rhythm, structure, and implication rather than simply extracting plot or argument. Confessional poetry — A mid-twentieth-century movement (Plath, Sexton, Lowell) that used highly personal, often painful autobiographical material as its primary subject. The term is a description, not a judgment. Dark Romanticism — A strand of nineteenth-century American writing (Hawthorne, Poe, Melville) that rejected the optimism of Transcendentalism and focused on sin, guilt, psychological complexity, and the uncanny. Double consciousness — W.E.B. Du Bois’s term for the experience of Black Americans who must see themselves simultaneously through their own eyes and through the eyes of a white society that regards them with contempt. Dunbar and Chesnutt embody it formally. Dramatic irony — When the reader knows something a character does not. Poe deploys it at the expense of his narrators. Free verse — Poetry without a fixed metrical pattern. Whitman is its great American pioneer; Williams extends the experiment into pure image. Gothic — A mode of writing that uses darkness, decay, secrecy, and psychological terror to explore what a culture represses or refuses to acknowledge. Harlem Renaissance — The flourishing of Black art, literature, and music centered in Harlem from approximately 1920 to 1940. More than a movement: a declaration of cultural citizenship. Image — A concrete sensory detail in a poem or prose that carries emotional and often symbolic weight. Williams’s wheelbarrow; Whitman’s wound; Dickinson’s fly; Hurston’s ships on the horizon. Naturalism — A late-nineteenth-century literary movement that applied the methods of natural science to fiction, depicting human beings as products of heredity, environment, and social forces largely beyond their control. Oral tradition — Literature transmitted through performance and memory rather than writing. The Indigenous texts in Sessions 1 and 16 originate here; what we read is a transcription of something that was always meant to be spoken. Persona — The voice or speaker of a poem, which may differ from the author. Plath’s mirror is a non-human persona; Chesnutt’s Uncle Julius is a fictional persona who tells a story within a story. Realism — A literary mode that seeks to represent life as it is actually lived, without idealization. Chopin and Gilman are realists who are also, in their different ways, early feminists. Rhetoric — The art of persuasion through language. Douglass, Lincoln, Paine, and King are all virtuoso rhetoricians. Understanding their specific choices helps you understand why they work. Transcendentalism — An American philosophical and literary movement of the 1830s–1850s that held that the individual soul has direct access to divine truth through nature and intuition, without the mediation of institutions or tradition. Voice — The distinctive personality and perspective that a writer projects through language. Voice is what makes a sentence unmistakably Whitman and not Dickinson — and what each writer in this course spent a lifetime learning to trust. Reading Companion ▾ How to Read American Literature There is a question underneath every text we will read this term, and it is not a literary question. It is a political one: Who gets to be American? Every generation of American writers has answered that question differently — or refused to answer it, or answered it and been ignored, or answered it and been punished for the answer. The history of American literature is, among other things, the history of that argument about belonging: who speaks, who is heard, who is written out of the record, and who writes themselves back in. The arc is not smooth or progressive. Writers who were central in their own time have been forgotten. Writers who were forgotten have been recovered. The canon is a negotiation that never ends, and we are part of it when we sit down to read. You do not need to know all of this in advance. But it helps to hold the question in mind, because it is almost always operating beneath the surface of even the most apparently private literary work. On reading poetry. Many people who love fiction feel uncertain about poetry, as though it requires a special training they lack. It does not. Poetry requires only what fiction requires — attention — plus one additional thing: a willingness to slow down further than you think is necessary. A poem wants to be read at least twice. The first time, let it wash over you. The second time, stop at anything that gives you a small shock — a surprise, a question, a confusion — and ask why the poet made that particular choice. The confusion is usually the poem. The place where you think you do not understand is almost always the place the poem is doing its most interesting work. On reading old texts. The earliest texts in this course were written in a different world. The Puritans believed things about God, salvation, and communal accountability that most of us do not share. Jefferson owned human beings while drafting a document about inalienable rights. Irving wrote in a comic register that can feel airless to modern ears. Do not let historical distance become an excuse to dismiss these writers. They are strange because they are from a different world — but it is our different world. We live in the consequences of their ideas. That is precisely what makes them worth the effort. On disagreeing. American literature is a contentious archive. Some of these writers will make you uncomfortable. Some of them contradict each other. Some said one thing and did another. The most useful response to discomfort is not to dismiss the text but to stay with the discomfort long enough to understand what it is telling you. The friction between what a text claims and what you know from your own life is not a problem to solve. It is the place where reading becomes thinking. On your own experience. You are not a blank slate who receives pure literary meaning from a text. You are a person who lives in Philadelphia in the twenty-first century, and everything you have seen and done and lost and hoped for is part of how you read. That is not a contamination of the reading experience. It is the reading experience. The writers in this course were also people who lived in particular places at particular times, with particular bodies and particular histories, and their particularity is what makes their writing matter. Yours does too. On what is missing. Any sixteen-week survey leaves out more than it includes. We do not read Melville, or Twain, or Henry James, or Willa Cather, or Richard Wright, or Ralph Ellison, or James Baldwin. We read almost no drama. We read very little fiction from the twentieth century’s second half. These are real absences, not oversights — we have to stop somewhere, and no stopping place is innocent. Consider this course a beginning, not a summary. Every writer we read is a door into a dozen writers we did not read. The Internet Archive is always three clicks away — free digital borrows, no library card required. A closing word. The great project of American literature, taken as a whole, is an argument about what this country could be — and a reckoning with what it has done and failed to do. The most honest texts hold both sides of that story at once: the aspiration and the failure, the speech and the silence beneath it, the dream and the long, difficult morning after. To read that literature attentively — to sit with Douglass and Dickinson and Hurston in the same room and ask what they have to say to each other — is not an academic exercise. It is a way of understanding where you live, and why, and what you might do with the time you have here. I am glad you are here. Let us begin. About Me ▾ I am James F. Mulhern — a Philadelphia writer and teacher. I taught English at the secondary and college levels for more than thirty years and served as Department Chair. I was awarded a fully funded Writing Fellowship at Exeter College, University of Oxford — a grant that brought together writers selected from around the world — and have written fiction and essays that have appeared in literary journals in the United States and abroad. I offer this course because I believe that literary education should not end when formal schooling ends — and because the best literary conversations I have had in my life have not happened in classrooms. They have happened in rooms like this one, among people who have no obligation to be there except their own curiosity. You can reach me by email at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com , or through the course site at art-of-telling.com . I look forward to reading with you. About the Use of These Materials ▾ These materials — course descriptions, reading lists, syllabi, discussion questions, session pages, and prompts — were written and designed by James F. Mulhern for Silver Current Press. Readers are welcome to read, print, share, and quote them for personal use and study. Teachers, program directors, and institutions who would like to use any of this material in a classroom, syllabus, publication, or paid program are asked to write first — a short email is enough. The answer will almost always be a warm yes, with a note on attribution. Please contact Professor Mulhern at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . The Sessions ▾ Session One — The First Voices Session Two — The Errand into the Wilderness Session Three — The Language of Liberty Session Four — The Counter-Narrative Session Five — The Self in Nature Session Six — The American Gothic Session Seven — War, Justice, and Prose Session Eight — War, Mourning, and Poetry Session Nine — Confinement and Its Names Session Ten — The Mask and the Story Session Eleven — The Voice in the Wall Session Twelve — The Image on the Street Session Thirteen — Defiance and the Dream Session Fourteen — Joy, Folk, and the Interior Life Session Fifteen — The Private Made Public Session Sixteen — Here, Now: Capstone ‹ Close Session One — The First Voices Pre-Colonial Literature | Week 1 Main Points of the Lesson American literature does not begin with the colonists. It begins thousands of years earlier, in the oral traditions of peoples who were already here. To start the survey with the Iroquois, Ojibwe, and Cherokee is to refuse the convenient fiction that the story opens with arriving Europeans. These are stories built for the ear, not the page. What we read is a transcription — usually made by an outside observer — of something that was always meant to be spoken aloud, remembered, and performed. The form on the page is a translation already at one remove from the living thing. The cosmology is rel

title: The Art of Telling · The 2601 Salon
heading: The Art of Telling
description: A ten-session salon in short story, poetry, and memoir — the course that gave the salon its name.
text: The Art of Telling · The 2601 Salon The 2601 Salon For Partners Table of Contents Courses Formats Philosophy Thin Places Enroll or Book For program partners: This course can be brought to any adult reading audience — in person or on Zoom. See the partners page or download a one-page flyer for this course . Notices & Announcements Posted Current Welcome to The 2601 Salon — a working catalog of literary courses for adult readers and writers, offered in person or on Zoom. To learn more, express interest, or bring a course to your venue, email Professor Mulhern at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . The Whiteboard is available on every course page for live in-class notes. The Art of Telling Ten Sessions A literary course for adult readers and writers · taught by James F. Mulhern ‹ Back to all courses What would you like to see? Click any button below. Important Information & Course Materials ▾ An Invitation ▾ For ten Sundays we sit together and read three of the great rooms of literature — the short story, the poem, the memoir — and let them speak to us in turn. This is the course that gave the salon its name. It was first offered over ten Sunday afternoons and it went so well that it belongs on the shelf beside the other courses — available to any adult reader who wants to sit down with three genres at once and see how they answer each other. You do not need to have been in the original room to take this course. Everything the course teaches is in the readings, in the questions, and in the writing you do by hand, on paper, in the company of fellow readers. Welcome ▾ Welcome to The Art of Telling — a ten-session course for adult readers and writers who want to read, and write, across the three great narrative forms. Over ten weeks we will read one story a week, then move to poetry, then to memoir. We will read aloud. We will slow down. We will ask, of every text, the same set of small honest questions: What is happening in this sentence? What is the writer withholding? What is the last paragraph doing? And what would happen if we tried a paragraph of our own in that mode? Every session runs ninety minutes. The course is non-graded and non-competitive. Nothing you write is collected or evaluated. Nothing leaves the room unless you choose to take it home. What This Course Is ▾ This is a reading-and-writing salon for adults who want to understand how the modern short story, the contemporary poem, and the American memoir actually work — and who want to try writing in those forms themselves. Each session, we will: Read one text aloud together — a short story, a set of poems, or a memoir passage. Discuss what the writer is doing, in plain language, without jargon. Practice one craft element through a brief in-class writing exercise, by hand. Take home an optional longer prompt to work on between sessions. The three units are proportioned to the tradition. Four sessions on the short story. Three sessions on poetry. Three sessions on memoir. A short farewell session on the writing life. The emphasis is on craft : on how writers make the small choices — a verb, a line break, a scene, a piece of silence — that turn material into literature. We read to become better writers. We write to become better readers. What This Course Is Not ▾ It is not a lecture course. I will talk, but so will you. The best learning in this room will come from conversation. It is not a competitive workshop. No one’s writing will be criticized, ranked, or compared. It is not a book club. We read for craft, not only for pleasure. It is not a commitment to publish. Whatever you write belongs entirely to you. It is not graded. There are no wrong answers to any of the discussion questions. It is not required. Come when you can. Read what you are able. Write what feels right. About the Instructor ▾ James F. Mulhern is a Professor of English and a former Department Chair, and is the recipient of a fully funded Writing Fellowship at Exeter College, University of Oxford. His novel Give Them Unquiet Dreams received a Kirkus starred review and was named a Kirkus Best Book of 2019. He is the founder of Silver Current Press, a Philadelphia literary imprint. He has taught writing at the university level for many years and believes, without reservation, that reading and writing are the same craft practiced from two ends. He lives in Philadelphia. Course Details ▾ Course Title The Art of Telling: A Salon in Short Story, Poetry, and Memoir Instructor James F. Mulhern Format In person or on Zoom Meeting Length 90 minutes Duration Ten sessions Cost Contact for current terms Class Size Open enrollment Materials Pen and paper Grading None What to Expect Each Week ▾ Each session follows the same shape, so you always know what is coming: A short welcome and one small idea to hold in mind. A close reading of the week’s text, aloud, together. A discussion — questions from me, questions from you, silences where they belong. Ten minutes of writing by hand, from a single prompt. A short farewell and the next week’s reading. If you cannot attend a session, you have not missed the course. Rejoin the next week. The salon is designed to survive absence. Readings ▾ All texts are available free online. Every session page in the original salon links directly to a public-domain or open-access version of the reading. No book purchase is required. A Companion Volume ▾ Because ten Sundays turned out to be too short to say everything the course wanted to say, a companion volume was written after the fact and lives on its own website: companion.art-of-telling.com . It contains, for each of the ten sessions, an expanded biography of the writer, a fuller close reading, historical and political context, answers to every discussion question, and a longer craft essay. You can read it online or download the sixty-eight-page Word booklet from the site. Anyone taking the course a second time — or coming to it for the first time on the shelf — is welcome to use the companion as a study guide. A Few Promises ▾ Every text will be short enough to read carefully in one week. Every session will end on time. No one will ever be forced to read their writing aloud. The room will be quiet enough to think in. I will not talk down to anyone in the room. A Few Asks ▾ Come with the reading done, if you can. If you cannot, come anyway. Bring a pen and a notebook. Do not use your phone in the room. The room is one of the last places you can put it down. Be generous with your fellow readers’ pages. That is the whole practice. Registration ▾ There is no formal registration. Send a note to Professor Mulhern to let him know you plan to attend, and a seat will be waiting. Please email james@silvercurrentpress.com to reserve a seat, ask a question, or request a copy of the course reading list in advance. The Art of Telling — a salon in short story, poetry, and memoir, for adult readers and writers. About the Use of These Materials ▾ These materials — course descriptions, reading lists, syllabi, discussion questions, session pages, and prompts — were written and designed by James F. Mulhern for Silver Current Press. Readers are welcome to read, print, share, and quote them for personal use and study. Teachers, program directors, and institutions who would like to use any of this material in a classroom, syllabus, publication, or paid program are asked to write first — a short email is enough. The answer will almost always be a warm yes, with a note on attribution. Please contact Professor Mulhern at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . The Sessions ▾ Session 1 — What Is a Story? Session 2 — The Seven Questions Every Story Must Answer Session 3 — Scene & Summary Session 4 — Character & Desire Session 5 — Image & the Poetic Line Session 6 — Voice & the Lyric "I" Session 7 — Compression Session 8 — Memory & the Memoir Impulse Session 9 — The Double Structure Session 10 — Revision: How Writers Re-See ‹ Close Session 1 — What Is a Story? Focus: The shape of the modern short story. What a story does and does not need. We begin with a story that famously withholds almost everything — dialogue only, no interior thought, no exposition — and ask what a story really is when almost everything conventional has been taken away. Main Points of the Lesson A story is a shape, not a subject. What makes fiction a story is not the topic but the arc — a change, however small, in a character or a situation between the first sentence and the last. The modern story trusts the reader. From Chekhov onward, the story leaves out more than it says. What the reader supplies from a well-placed detail is often more powerful than what the writer supplies from an explanation. Dialogue can do the work of exposition. Hemingway’s story is almost entirely dialogue, yet by the end we know the two characters, the situation, and the emotional stakes. The last sentence bears extra weight. Story endings are not resolutions; they are placements. The final image is what the reader carries out of the room. The modern story is short by design, not by accident. Compression is a positive craft choice, not a limitation. Reading Ernest Hemingway, “Hills Like White Elephants” (1927) — Great Books Foundation (PDF) In-Class Practice Read the story aloud, then in pairs. Circle every line of dialogue that carries information the narrator does not otherwise supply. Discuss what the story assumes we can figure out. (10 minutes.) Discussion Questions What is the “elephant” in the story? Does the story name it? Why not? How does Hemingway make you feel the tension between the two characters without ever describing what either one thinks? What is the effect of the setting — the train station, the two sets of tracks, the hills — on the meaning of the story? Whose story is this? The man’s, the woman’s, or the couple’s? Change any one line of dialogue. What breaks? Homework Write a two-page story that is at least eighty percent dialogue, in which two characters discuss something they cannot bring themselves to name. Bring it next week. ‹ Close Session 2 — The Seven Questions Every Story Must Answer Focus: Point of view, desire, obstacle, choice, consequence, image, and last paragraph. Using Gilman’s uncanny story of a woman losing her mind (or seeing more clearly than everyone around her), we develop the seven-question checklist that every story, in some form, must resolve. Main Points of the Lesson Every story has a point of view — even omniscient ones. The angle from which the story is told is a moral position, not just a technical choice. Every story has a desire and an obstacle. No matter how quiet, a story tracks something a character wants and something between the character and that wanting. Every story turns on a choice. The character does something the reader has been prepared to feel the weight of. Every story pays a consequence. The choice has a cost the story is willing to show. Every story rides an image. One recurring picture carries the emotional weight the language cannot say directly. In Gilman, it is the wallpaper. The last paragraph is the paragraph the whole story was written for. Read it first. Write your story toward it. Reading Charlotte Perkins Gilman, “The Yellow Wallpaper” (1892) — Project Gutenberg Critical Reception Charlotte Perkins Gilman — Poetry Foundation biographical entry — for context on Gilman’s public feminism and the personal experience that produced this story. In-Class Practice Take a story you have written or drafted and answer the seven questions on paper. Any question you cannot answer confidently is a place your story is not yet finished. (10 minutes.) Discussion Questions Whose story is this — the wife’s, the husband’s, or the wallpaper’s? When does the narrator’s reliability change for you as a reader? Which sentence is the tipping point? What is the story’s image, and how does it evolve from opening to close? Read the last paragraph aloud. Now read the first paragraph. What has changed? If Gilman had written this as a first-person recollection years later (“I once lived in a house…”), how would the story change? Homework Read a story you love. Answer the seven questions of that story on paper. Bring your notes; the class will pool what different readers found. ‹ Close Session 3 — Scene & Summary Focus: When to slow the story down. When to speed it up. Free indirect discourse. Mansfield’s braided family portrait is one of the great examples of a story that knows exactly when to be inside a character’s head and exactly when to zoom back out. Main Points of the Lesson Scene shows; summary tells. Both are necessary. The craft is knowing when each is the right tool. Scene is what the reader will remember. Every important turn of a story should happen in scene. Summary handles time. Weeks and years compress into a paragraph; the reader trusts the compression when the scenes that anchor it are strong. Free indirect discourse is the great modern innovation. The narrator borrows a character’s diction and rhythm without the marker of “she thought.” Reader and character briefly share one voice. Rhythm inside a story matters. The alternation of scene and summary is a story’s heartbeat. Reading Katherine Mansfield, “At the Bay” (1922) — University of Adelaide edition Critical Reception Katherine Mansfield — Poetry Foundation biographical entry — background on Mansfield’s modernist innovations and her influence on the twentieth-century short story. In-Class Practice Take a paragraph you have written. Mark it S for scene or U for summary line by line. Where does the story live? Where does it move? (5 minutes.) Discussion Questions Where in “At the Bay” does the narrator briefly borrow a character’s inner voice? Choose one moment and read it aloud. Which character in the family did the story make you love most? Why? What did Mansfield do to make you love them? What does the sea do in this story? The story has no plot in the traditional sense. What holds it together? If you were adapting this story for the screen, which paragraph would you insist on preserving as-is? Homework Write a two-page scene followed by a one-paragraph summary that covers a week of story time. Bring it in. ‹ Close Session 4 — Character & Desire Focus: The character who does not know what she wants until the story reveals it. Chekhov’s late masterpiece is the most influential short story in modern literature. It also happens to be about two people who do not admit, until it is too late, that they love each other. Main Points of the Lesson Character is desire made specific. A character without a want is a character without a shape. The most powerful desires are the ones the character will not name. Chekhov’s story is about two people whose stated desire (an affair) is a mask for a desire they cannot yet say (a life together). A story often reveals its character to us before revealing it to the character. The reader sees Gurov change before Gurov does. Chekhov’s endings do not resolve — they open. The story ends where the difficult work begins. The great short-story writers write as if they know what will happen next but decline to tell us. They give us enough to imagine it. Reading Anton Chekhov, “The Lady with the Dog” (1899) — Bartleby full text or Project Gutenberg selected stories Critical Reception Anton Chekhov — Poetry Foundation biographical entry — a portrait of the writer widely credited with inventing the modern short story. In-Class Practice Write down what Gurov wants in three registers: (1) what he tells himself, (2) what he tells Anna, (3) what the story tells us. Where do the three disagree? (5 minutes.) Discussion Questions When does Gurov change? Point to a specific sentence. What does the dog do in the story, and why does Chekhov keep bringing it up? The story is set in Yalta, Moscow, and the provincial town where Anna lives. What does each place do to the characters? The story ends without resolution. Is that satisfying? Why or why not? Chekhov famously said that the writer’s job is not to solve problems but to state them correctly. Where in this story does he state a problem exactly right? Homework Take a character in your own writing and answer, on paper: what do they say they want, and what do they actually want? Write a scene that turns on the difference. ‹ Close Session 5 — Image & the Poetic Line Focus: Where the poem breaks and why. We begin the poetry unit by looking at four poets who trust the concrete image and shape the poem line by line. Bishop, Frost, Williams, and Oliver — very different writers who share one belief: that the poem lives in what you can see. Main Points of the Lesson A poem’s line is a unit of meaning. Every line is a small decision about what the reader takes in at once. The image is the fastest way into a poem. A concrete picture reaches a reader before an abstract statement can. Enjambment is a rhythmic weapon. Where a line breaks changes what the sentence emphasizes. The first line makes a contract with the reader. The rest of the poem either honors it, adjusts it, or breaks it deliberately. Reading aloud reveals the poem’s shape. The eye can miss what the ear catches on the first pass. Reading Elizabeth Bishop, “One Art” — Poetry Foundation Robert Frost, “Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening” — Poetry Foundation William Carlos Williams, “This Is Just to Say” — Poetry Foundation Mary Oliver, “Wild Geese” — The Marginalian In-Class Practice Read each poem aloud. On a second reading, mark the enjambments (lines that break in the middle of a syntactic unit). Note which enjambments create surprise and which create emphasis. (10 minutes.) Discussion Questions What is Bishop’s poem actually about? Is “the art of losing” mastered by the end? What is Frost’s poem “really” about — sleep, death, or the responsibility to keep going? Or all three? Williams’s poem is a note left on a refrigerator. Is it a poem? What makes it one? What does Oliver’s “You do not have to be good” do that a direct statement would not? Choose one poem. Rewrite it as prose. What did the line breaks give the poem that the prose loses? Homework Write a twelve-line poem in free verse in which each line contains one concrete image. Bring it in. ‹ Close Session 6 — Voice & the Lyric "I" Focus: Who is speaking. To whom. From what distance. The lyric “I” is not a diary; it is a mask carefully worn. This session reads three poets — Heaney, Kenyon, Clifton — whose speakers are unmistakable, and asks what makes a voice on the page unmistakable at all. Main Points of the Lesson The lyric “I” is a persona, not an autobiography. Even the most personal-sounding poem has been made — chosen, shaped, revised. Voice is a bundle of habits. Diction, syntax, rhythm, punctuation, silence. What a voice does not do is often more identifying than what it does. Every speaker has an implied listener. Some poems address a lover, some a reader, some a self, some a God. The address shapes the meaning. Distance matters. The speaker can be inside the moment, remembering it, dreaming it, or preparing to write about it. Each distance produces a different poem. Voice is the closest thing poetry has to a plot. It is what carries a lyric through. Reading Seamus Heaney, “Digging” — Poetry Foundation Jane Kenyon, “Otherwise” — Poetry Foundation Lucille Clifton, “won’t you celebrate with me” — Poetry Foundation In-Class Practice Read each poem aloud, then trade poems and read a stranger’s aloud. What changes when a voice not your own says these lines? (5–10 minutes.) Discussion Questions Whose voice is Heaney’s speaker in “Digging”? Is he the boy at the window, or the man remembering the boy? Kenyon’s poem repeats the phrase “It might have been otherwise.” What does the repetition do to the poem’s emotional temperature? Clifton’s poem is fourteen lines and eighty-eight syllables. What makes it feel bigger than that? Choose one of the three speakers. Where in your life have you heard a voice like that speaker’s? What made you

title: How Chekhov Ends · The 2601 Salon
heading: How Chekhov Ends
description: A four-session close-reading workshop on the last paragraph of the modern short story, taught by James F. Mulhern — offered in person or online.
text: How Chekhov Ends · The 2601 Salon The 2601 Salon For Partners Table of Contents Courses Formats Philosophy Thin Places Enroll or Book For program partners: This course can be brought to any adult reading audience — in person or on Zoom. See the partners page or download a one-page flyer for this course . Notices & Announcements Posted Current Welcome to The 2601 Salon — a working catalog of literary courses for adult readers and writers, offered in person or on Zoom. To learn more, express interest, or bring a course to your venue, email Professor Mulhern at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . The Whiteboard is available on every course page for live in-class notes. How Chekhov Ends Four Sessions A literary course for adult readers and writers · taught by James F. Mulhern ‹ Back to all courses What would you like to see? Click any button below. Important Information & Course Materials ▾ An Invitation ▾ Anton Chekhov did not invent the modern short story, but he did teach it how to end. Before Chekhov, a story reached a moral. After Chekhov, a story opens a room and lets the reader stand in it. The last paragraph became the paragraph the whole story was written for — the one that does not resolve, but places. This four-session workshop reads four of Chekhov’s finest late stories with a single question in front of us: what does the last paragraph do? We read the story once for its own sake, then we read the ending again — three or four times — and we talk about what Chekhov made possible for every writer who followed him. The workshop is for adult readers who love short fiction, for writers who want their own stories to end more truthfully, and for anyone who has ever finished a Chekhov story and sat still for a long minute before putting the book down. What This Course Is ▾ A four-session close-reading workshop One story per session, all by Chekhov, all available free online Ninety minutes per session, discussion-based, no lecture Non-graded, non-competitive, open to any adult reader In person or on Zoom, adaptable to any partner venue’s calendar What This Course Is Not ▾ Not a survey of Chekhov’s life or his plays Not a Russian-language course (all readings are in the best English translations) Not a writing workshop (though writers are especially welcome) Not a book club (we read closely, sentence by sentence, at the end) About the Instructor ▾ James F. Mulhern is a Kirkus-starred novelist, Oxford Writing Fellow, and Professor Emeritus of English with more than thirty years of teaching experience. He has taught Chekhov at the college and graduate levels and has taught weekend Chekhov intensives for adult reading groups. His novel Give Them Unquiet Dreams received a starred review from Kirkus Reviews and was named a Kirkus Best Book of 2019. Course Details ▾ Instructor: James F. Mulhern Location: in person or on Zoom Format: Weekly, 90 minutes per session Duration: 4 weeks Cost: Contact for current terms Enrollment: Open to all adults; no application required Grading: None Required texts: None to purchase. All readings are free and linked in this document. Materials to bring: This document (printed or on your phone/tablet), something to write with, and something to write on What to Expect Each Week ▾ Each session follows the same shape: Read aloud — we begin with someone reading the story aloud, or the ending aloud if the story is long First response — we talk about what struck each of us on first reading Close reading of the ending — the final paragraph, sentence by sentence, three or four passes The Chekhov question — what did the ending make possible? What did it foreclose? Craft takeaway — one thing writers can learn from this ending Readings ▾ All texts are available free online. Every session page links to a public-domain or open-access version of the reading. No book purchase is required. A Companion Volume ▾ Coming soon — a companion volume of Chekhov’s endings, side-by-side, with James F. Mulhern’s marginal notes. A Few Promises ▾ Every session begins on time and ends on time. Every discussion is generous. Nothing anyone says in the room is repeated outside it. No one is asked to speak. Silence is a legitimate contribution. The reading is short enough for anyone with a busy life to finish before the session. A Few Asks ▾ Read the story before the session. Ninety minutes is not enough to read and discuss. Bring the printed or digital story with you. We refer to it constantly. Come to as many sessions as you can, but come when you can. A missed session is not a lost seat. Registration ▾ To register or to bring this course to a partner venue, please email jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . The course can be delivered as a four-session workshop, a single weekend intensive (two half-day sessions), or four evening lectures in a row. About the Use of These Materials ▾ These materials — course descriptions, reading lists, syllabi, discussion questions, session pages, and prompts — were written and designed by James F. Mulhern for Silver Current Press. Readers are welcome to read, print, share, and quote them for personal use and study. Teachers, program directors, and institutions who would like to use any of this material in a classroom, syllabus, publication, or paid program are asked to write first — a short email is enough. The answer will almost always be a warm yes, with a note on attribution. Please contact Professor Mulhern at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . The Sessions ▾ Session 1 — "The Lady with the Dog" Session 2 — "The Bishop" Session 3 — "Gooseberries" Session 4 — "A Day in the Country" and Reflection ‹ Close Session 1 — "The Lady with the Dog" Focus: The story often cited as the founding text of the modern short story. Two people who cannot admit they love each other. Chekhov ends where the difficult work begins. Main Points of the Lesson The Chekhov ending does not resolve — it opens. The story stops where the next chapter of the characters’ lives would begin. The reader is trusted. Chekhov gives us what we need to imagine the rest, and no more. The last image carries the emotional weight. In this story, it is the “long, long way still to go.” The ending validates every ambiguity the story built. Every uncertainty in the middle is answered, in a Chekhov ending, not by resolution but by acceptance. Compare with the traditional Victorian ending. Where Dickens closes the door, Chekhov opens the window. Reading Anton Chekhov, “The Lady with the Dog” (1899) — Project Gutenberg Critical Reception Anton Chekhov — Poetry Foundation biographical entry — a portrait of the writer widely credited with inventing the modern short story. In-Class Practice Read the last paragraph aloud. Now change the very last sentence — write any alternate ending. Read both aloud. What breaks? What is preserved? (10 minutes.) Discussion Questions Read the final paragraph. What is Chekhov not saying? Compare Gurov at the beginning of the story to Gurov at the end. What has changed? Which sentence marks the change? What does the dog do in the ending? Why does Chekhov not mention it? Is this a story about love, about age, or about self-knowledge? Or all three? If you were told this story ended in a marriage, would you believe the story? Why or why not? Homework Read the last paragraphs of two other Chekhov stories you know or find. Bring your favorite closing sentence next week. ‹ Close Session 2 — "The Bishop" Focus: A dying bishop remembers his mother. Chekhov’s most tender ending — a story that ends in the moment after death without ever describing it. Main Points of the Lesson Chekhov’s endings hold suffering without dramatizing it. The bishop’s death is a fact, not a scene. Time expands in the last paragraph. What took the whole story to earn takes one paragraph to release. The ending shifts perspective. We leave the bishop and see the world after him — the peasants gathering, the ordinary morning. This is one of Chekhov’s most powerful moves. A great ending redistributes the weight of the story. Every detail earlier — the mother’s visit, the bishop’s uncertainty, his exhaustion — is repaid. The ending affirms the reader. After a Chekhov ending, the reader is different. Reading Anton Chekhov, “The Bishop” (1902) — Project Gutenberg (in the collection The Bishop and Other Stories) In-Class Practice Rewrite the last paragraph so that the bishop’s death is shown rather than passed over. What does the story lose? What might it gain? (10 minutes.) Discussion Questions Chekhov ends the story with the bishop’s mother telling the story of her son. What does that do? Notice the passage of time in the last two paragraphs. How much time passes? How does Chekhov compress it? Read the story’s opening sentence and its closing sentence. What is the relationship between them? This story is often called Chekhov’s most religious. Is it religious? What does “religious” mean here? If you were writing an obituary for the bishop, what would you include that Chekhov leaves out? Homework Write a short piece (a page) whose final paragraph moves the point of view from a single character to the world around them. Bring it in. ‹ Close Session 3 — "Gooseberries" Focus: A story-within-a-story about a man who spent his life pursuing his idea of happiness. Chekhov’s most morally charged ending — a story that turns the reader into the subject of the story. Main Points of the Lesson The Chekhov ending can implicate the reader. By the last paragraph of “Gooseberries,” the frame narrator is no longer sure of anything, and neither are we. A story can end with a question. Not a rhetorical one — a real one that the reader is left to answer. The ending can reveal the story was about something else. We think this is a story about the brother in the country; we discover it is a story about all of us. Chekhov’s morality is never a moral. He refuses to tell us what to think but insists that we think. Contrast this with a Tolstoyan ending. Tolstoy tells us what the story means. Chekhov trusts us to find it. Reading Anton Chekhov, “Gooseberries” (1898) — Project Gutenberg (in The Wife and Other Stories) In-Class Practice Underline every sentence in the last two pages that could be a moral. What does Chekhov do with each? (5 minutes.) Discussion Questions Who is speaking in the last paragraph? Ivan Ivanich or the frame narrator? Or someone else? What is the “gooseberries” of the title? What does the fruit represent by the last paragraph? The story ends with rain. What does the rain do? Is this a story about a bad man (the brother)? Or about a whole class of people? Or about the whole species? Chekhov leaves all three doors open. Which one do you walk through? Write down the last sentence. Read it three times. What does it ask of you? Homework Take a story of your own that ends with a resolution. Rewrite the ending so it ends with a question the reader must answer. ‹ Close Session 4 — "A Day in the Country" and Reflection Focus: A shorter, less anthologized Chekhov story about a shoemaker and two children in a summer thunderstorm. Chekhov at his most compressed and generous. We end the workshop with this story and then a group reflection on what we have learned about endings. Main Points of the Lesson A Chekhov ending can be joyful. Not every one is a farewell. The shortest Chekhov stories often carry the longest afterlives. Compression is a positive craft choice. The ending returns us to the ordinary world with new eyes. This is what many great endings do — return us, changed. All four endings we have read share one gesture: they place the reader inside the story rather than outside it looking in. A writer’s endings are the writer’s signature. Chekhov’s signature is trust — in the material, in the reader, in silence. Reading Anton Chekhov, “A Day in the Country” (1886) — Eldritch Press full text In-Class Practice Group exercise: each person shares one sentence — the closing sentence — from a favorite short story (Chekhov or not). We read them aloud. What do they share? What do they refuse to share? (15 minutes.) Discussion Questions What does the thunderstorm do at the end? This is a shorter and sunnier story than the others. What Chekhovian gesture does it still make? Compare the last paragraphs of the four stories we have read. What is the same? What is different? If Chekhov taught you one thing about how to end a story, what would you say it is? Which of the four endings will you remember longest? Why? Homework None. Instead: read a Chekhov story you have never read before — there are more than three hundred — and see if the ending does what we have been discussing. title: Reading Dickinson · The 2601 Salon
heading: Reading Dickinson
description: A four-session close-reading of Emily Dickinson's poems — interior landscapes, poems on death, nature, and the great late lyrics, taught by James F. Mulhern.
text: Reading Dickinson · The 2601 Salon The 2601 Salon For Partners Table of Contents Courses Formats Philosophy Thin Places Enroll or Book For program partners: This course can be brought to any adult reading audience — in person or on Zoom. See the partners page or download a one-page flyer for this course . Notices & Announcements Posted Current Welcome to The 2601 Salon — a working catalog of literary courses for adult readers and writers, offered in person or on Zoom. To learn more, express interest, or bring a course to your venue, email Professor Mulhern at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . The Whiteboard is available on every course page for live in-class notes. Reading Dickinson Four Sessions A literary course for adult readers and writers · taught by James F. Mulhern ‹ Back to all courses What would you like to see? Click any button below. Important Information & Course Materials ▾ An Invitation ▾ Emily Dickinson wrote nearly eighteen hundred poems. She published seven while she lived. She sewed the rest into small hand-stitched fascicles and left them in a drawer. When they emerged after her death, English poetry had to reorganize itself around them. This four-session course reads Dickinson slowly. Six or seven poems per session — no more — and only the poems that reward the closest attention. Her dashes. Her capitalization. Her rhymes that almost rhyme but don’t. Her small stanzas that contain more universe than anyone else’s whole books. This is a course for readers who have always been a little afraid of Dickinson, or who admire her from a distance and want to come closer. No prior reading of Dickinson is required. We move at the pace of the poems. What This Course Is ▾ A four-session close-reading course Six to seven Dickinson poems per session Ninety minutes per session, discussion-based Non-graded, non-competitive, open to any adult reader In person or on Zoom, adaptable to any partner venue’s calendar What This Course Is Not ▾ Not a biography of Dickinson (her life is fascinating but is not the subject) Not a survey of nineteenth-century American poetry (Dickinson is her own century) Not a poetry-writing workshop (though Dickinson’s craft lessons are inescapable) About the Instructor ▾ James F. Mulhern is a Kirkus-starred novelist, Oxford Writing Fellow, poet, and Professor Emeritus of English. He has taught Dickinson at every level, from high school AP classes to graduate seminars, and considers her the finest American lyric poet. His own poetry has been shortlisted for the Aesthetica Creative Writing Award. Course Details ▾ Instructor: James F. Mulhern Location: in person or on Zoom Format: Weekly, 90 minutes per session Duration: 4 weeks Cost: Contact for current terms Enrollment: Open to all adults; no application required Grading: None Required texts: None to purchase. All poems are free and linked in this document. Materials to bring: This document (printed or on your phone/tablet), and something to write with What to Expect Each Week ▾ Each session follows the same shape: Read aloud — every poem is read aloud by different readers before we discuss First response — what the poem gave you before you thought about it Close reading — line by line, stanza by stanza The Dickinson question — what did she do here that no one before her had done? Craft takeaway — one move a writer can carry away Readings ▾ All texts are available free online through the Poetry Foundation. No book purchase is required. A Companion Volume ▾ Coming soon — an annotated Dickinson reader with James F. Mulhern’s marginal notes. A Few Promises ▾ Every session begins on time and ends on time. Every discussion is generous. Nothing said in the room leaves it. No one is asked to speak. Silence is a legitimate contribution. Dickinson is compressed on the page but generous in the room. We move slowly. A Few Asks ▾ Read the poems before the session. They are short; read each one twice. Bring the printed or digital text. We refer to specific lines constantly. Come to as many sessions as you can. Each session widens the last. Registration ▾ To register or bring this course to a partner venue — libraries, museums, universities, retirement communities — please email jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . About the Use of These Materials ▾ These materials — course descriptions, reading lists, syllabi, discussion questions, session pages, and prompts — were written and designed by James F. Mulhern for Silver Current Press. Readers are welcome to read, print, share, and quote them for personal use and study. Teachers, program directors, and institutions who would like to use any of this material in a classroom, syllabus, publication, or paid program are asked to write first — a short email is enough. The answer will almost always be a warm yes, with a note on attribution. Please contact Professor Mulhern at jamesfmulhern@gmail.com . The Sessions ▾ Session 1 — Dickinson's Small Rooms: Interior Landscapes Session 2 — Death Is Her Subject: Dickinson on Mortality Session 3 — Nature and the Wild: Dickinson Outdoors Session 4 — The Great Late Poems: Dickinson in Command ‹ Close Session 1 — Dickinson's Small Rooms: Interior Landscapes Focus: Six poems set inside a single consciousness. The mind at its smallest scale, seen with unforgiving clarity. Dickinson’s great subject: the room inside the room inside the head. Main Points of the Lesson Dickinson’s compression is technique, not shortage. She said as much as she could fit in the smallest possible space — the opposite of Whitman. The dash is a Dickinson invention. It is not a comma, not a period, not a colon. It is a caesura and a hesitation and a leap all at once. Capitalization signals mid-line emphasis. Nouns capitalized are nouns Dickinson thinks the reader is looking at wrong. Slant rhyme is a Dickinson signature. She rhymes “fly” with “die” but also “soul” with “all.” The near-miss produces the emotional charge. The interior is her territory. No American poet before her — and few since — has mapped the small room of the mind so completely. Reading “I felt a Funeral, in my Brain” (280) — Poetry Foundation “The Soul selects her own Society” (303) — Poetry Foundation “There’s a certain Slant of light” (258) — Poetry Foundation “Much Madness is divinest Sense” (435) — Poetry Foundation “I dwell in Possibility” (657) — Poetry Foundation “The Brain is wider than the Sky” (632) — Poetry Foundation Critical Reception Emily Dickinson — Poetry Foundation biographical entry — the standard scholarly starting point. In-Class Practice Take “I felt a Funeral, in my Brain.” Read it aloud three times, each time emphasizing a different word in the first line. What changes each time? (10 minutes.) Discussion Questions What does the dash do at the end of a Dickinson line? Try reading a poem aloud replacing every dash with a period. What breaks? In “The Soul selects her own Society,” who or what is being shut out? Who is being kept in? “Much Madness is divinest Sense” — is this an argument, a lament, or a joke? Read “I dwell in Possibility” and “The Brain is wider than the Sky” back to back. What do they say together that neither says alone? Choose one poem from the six. Rewrite it without dashes and without capitals. What does Dickinson gain by breaking convention? Homework Read three more Dickinson poems on your own. Bring your favorite line to the next session. ‹ Close Session 2 — Death Is Her Subject: Dickinson on Mortality Focus: Nearly a third of Dickinson’s poems concern death, and no American poet has read the subject so calmly. This session takes six poems where Dickinson approaches death as an interlocutor — not a horror, not a comfort, but a companion. Main Points of the Lesson Dickinson does not flinch. She looks directly at death. This is uncommon in the poetry of her century and rare in ours. She personifies death without sentimentalizing it. Death in Dickinson is a courteous carriage-driver, a fly, a house, a school. The plainness of her language conceals the depth of her thought. “Because I could not stop for Death” begins as innocently as a nursery rhyme. Every death poem is a life poem. Dickinson uses death to see life more clearly — that’s the point. Her afterlife is uncertain, and she wants it that way. Where a lesser poet resolves, Dickinson leaves the question open. Reading “Because I could not stop for Death” (712) — Poetry Foundation “I heard a Fly buzz — when I died” (465) — Poetry Foundation “After great pain, a formal feeling comes” (341) — Poetry Foundation “Safe in their Alabaster Chambers” (216) — Poetry Foundation “This World is not Conclusion” (501) — Poetry Foundation “The Bustle in a House” (1078) — Poetry Foundation In-Class Practice Read “Because I could not stop for Death” aloud. Then read the last stanza only, aloud, three times. Where in that stanza does the poem’s whole meaning arrive? (10 minutes.) Discussion Questions What is the tone of “Because I could not stop for Death”? Is Dickinson afraid? Is she comforted? Is she something else? “I heard a Fly buzz” ends with “and then / I could not see to see.” What is that repetition doing? In “This World is not Conclusion,” Dickinson considers belief and unbelief in the same breath. Which side does she come down on? The last stanza of “The Bustle in a House” is one of the most quoted moments in American poetry. Read it aloud. What makes it hit so hard? If you were teaching one of these poems to a person who does not read poetry, which would you choose? Why? Homework Bring one Dickinson death poem we have not read. ‹ Close Session 3 — Nature and the Wild: Dickinson Outdoors Focus: Dickinson lived largely at home, but her poetry moves through birds, bees, flowers, and storms with unmatched intimacy. This session reads six poems in which she goes outside — sometimes into her Amherst garden, sometimes into weather that has never been named quite so well. Main Points of the Lesson Dickinson’s nature is close-up. No mountains. No sublime views. A single hummingbird. A single blade of grass. She resists the pastoral. Nature in Dickinson is unpredictable, sometimes menacing, often indifferent. The bird poems are theological. Dickinson does not use nature as decoration; she uses it as evidence. She names precisely. A bee is a bee. A snake is “a narrow Fellow in the Grass.” Precision is her spiritual practice. Nature in Dickinson does not console. It teaches — and its teaching is not always kind. Reading “A Bird, came down the Walk” (328) — Poetry Foundation “A narrow Fellow in the Grass” (986) — Poetry Foundation “‘Hope’ is the thing with feathers” (254) — Poetry Foundation “There came a Wind like a Bugle” (1593) — Poetry Foundation “I taste a liquor never brewed” (214) — Poetry Foundation “To make a prairie” (1755) — Poetry Foundation In-Class Practice Take “A Bird, came down the Walk.” Read it as a piece of prose reportage, sentence by sentence. Then read it again as a poem. What did Dickinson gain by making it a poem? (10 minutes.) Discussion Questions What is the mood of “A Bird, came down the Walk”? Where does it turn? Read “A narrow Fellow in the Grass” aloud. What is Dickinson doing with the word “Fellow”? Where else in the poem does language do double duty? “‘Hope’ is the thing with feathers” is one of her most-quoted poems. Is it also one of her strongest? Make the case. “To make a prairie” is four lines. Recite it. Then talk for ten minutes about it. What made ten minutes possible? Which of these poems most resists sentimentality? Which most invites it? Homework Look outside a window for five minutes. Then read “There came a Wind like a Bugle” again. What did you notice you had not noticed before? ‹ Close Session 4 — The Great Late Poems: Dickinson in Command Focus: By the 1870s Dickinson was writing poems that would define the reach of English poetry for the next hundred years. This session reads six of her most demanding, most rewarding poems — the ones she is still, more than a century later, teaching us how to read. Main Points of the Lesson Late Dickinson is Dickinson at maximum compression. These poems are so compact they seem to bend the air around them. The lyric self becomes multiple. Late Dickinson speaks from angles no other poet has taken. Her subjects grow larger — and her language grows smaller. She wrote about eternity in words a child could pronounce. Reading Dickinson well means reading her more than once. The first reading is the appetizer. The third is the meal. She is not a nineteenth-century poet. By the end of her life she is writing a twentieth-century poetry that America would not catch up to until Modernism. Reading “Tell all the truth but tell it slant” (1129) — Poetry Foundation “My life closed twice before its close” (1732) — Poetry Foundation “Wild nights - Wild nights!” (249) — Poetry Foundation “I cannot live with You” (640) — Poetry Foundation “Pain — has an Element of Blank” (650) — Poetry Foundation “Not knowing when the Dawn will come” (1619) — Poetry Foundation In-Class Practice Take “Tell all the truth but tell it slant.” Read it as a general reader would. Then read it as an ars poetica — a poem about how poems are made. What changes? (10 minutes.) Discussion Questions Read “My life closed twice before its close” aloud. What are the “two closings”? What is the third that has not yet come? “Wild nights - Wild nights!” is either a love poem, a religious poem, or both. Make the case for each reading. “I cannot live with You” is one of Dickinson’s longest poems. Where does the argument turn? Where does it climax? Where does it collapse? “Pain — has an Element of Blank” reads pain as a temporal phenomenon. What is she saying about pain and time? Which of the six poems is the hardest? Which is the easiest? Are you sure? Homework None. Instead: pick a Dickinson poem we have not read together and read it three times. Bring it to any conversation you have this week.
